How to read this book

This book runs on two assumptions about the world, and only two:

Axiom 1No one has perfect knowledge.

Axiom 2Mistakes are inevitable.

That is the entire list — and because everything downstream leans on these two sentences, they will return by name wherever a theorem stands on one of them. If you accept those two sentences — and no physicist, economist, priest, or skeptic can demonstrate or prove otherwise — then everything that follows is either derived from them or labeled as something less. (Every model in the book adds structure of its own — which signals exist, how errors correlate, what counts as survival — and each chapter’s §5 prints that structure and says what travels beyond it.) The labels are printed beside every claim:

  • PROVEN — a proof you can read, short enough to check by hand.
  • EXACT — computed by exhaustive enumeration, no sampling, no approximation.
  • NUMERICAL / MC / SIMULATION — computed with stated error, or by many simulated lifetimes with exact bookkeeping inside each; the weakest results in the book, and marked so.
  • DATA — measured in the world by someone else and tabulated here; descriptive unless a design is named, and never a proof of a model.
  • CONJECTURE — a potential pattern, not proven.
  • SPECULATIVE — an interesting idea, fenced off so it cannot pretend to be a result.
  • REFUTED — kept — something assumed a priori that the mathematics killed. There are several, and they are kept, because you may have had the same assumptions.

Every chapter is built the same way: §1–2 are for every reader; §3 onward for those who want the machinery; §6 for anyone who trusts nothing — the best kind of reader this book can have.

No rule. For every reader. This text runs straight down the page.

A blue rule. The machinery: theorems, mathematics, models. Folded shut; it opens where it stands.

A double brass rule. The receipts: code and records.

A dashed rule. Fenced: the one conjecture, on which nothing later depends.

And the book has two doors. Part I is the physics: the license under everything after it, in three short chapters. A reader who came for the schedule and not the particle can start at the harbor in Chapter 4 and miss nothing the measuring depends on; Chapter 3 says in one sentence what the physics contributes, and Part I is there whenever the license is questioned.

One more rule. The word theft appears throughout. It is defined mathematically in Chapter 7 — a measurable displacement, like a dent measured with calipers — before it is ever used as an accusation. If you dislike the word, strike it and read the equations. They do not change.

Part I. The Verdict and the Appeal · Chapter 1

The sealed verdict

There is a sentence that has been said to students, to prisoners, to employees, to whole populations, for about a century, always with the same borrowed confidence:

“Free will is an illusion.”

Notice what kind of sentence that is. It is not an argument — arguments can be answered. It is a claim of authority: somewhere, allegedly, in mathematics you have not read, the question was closed, and your protest is not a position but a symptom. You are, the sentence implies, a very complicated rock — and everything that follows from being a rock follows quietly: a rock cannot be robbed of choices it never had; a rock cannot be owed an education it could not use; what is done to a rock is arranged, not inflicted.

Living under an unanswerable sentence is a particular kind of confinement. This book calls it the sealed verdict: a judgment passed on your deepest nature, in a court you are forbidden to enter, delivered to you as final. Most people respond to a sealed verdict in one of two ways. They ignore it, and live as if free, with a small unpaid debt of doubt. Or they accept it, and discover that acceptance is oddly convenient for whoever is speaking.

There is a second sentence, politer, usually from kinder mouths, that does the same work by shrug instead of decree:

“It doesn’t matter whether you have free will or not.”

Notice what this one accomplishes. It concedes nothing and closes everything: no need to read the mathematics, because nothing allegedly hinges on it — live your life either way. The full answer to the second sentence is this entire book. The short answer: it matters, and it matters in the way things matter that can be counted. Whether a person’s actions are partly their own decides whether they can be robbed — whether taking their time, their options, their room to be wrong is an injury or merely a rearrangement of objects; whether an education is owed to something that could use one; whether what lands on a life was inflicted or just occurred. Every one of those questions turns out, in the chapters ahead, to be a measurable quantity with a price. And the shrug has been the accounting instrument by which that price is set to zero. “It doesn’t matter” is what it sounds like when the bill is being sent to someone else.

This book does not argue that you have free will. The wording is exact: it does not claim to prove freedom exists. No honest person currently can. What can be done — what has now been done, with theorems — is smaller and sharper: the authority of the sentence can be revoked. It can be shown, exactly, what physics does and does not require; it can be shown that the deterministic reading is a choice with a price sheet, not a conclusion with a proof; and it can be shown that the verdict was never entered — that at every size at which the question has been priced, the universe declines to sign it.

Revoking an authority is not a metaphorical act. It requires arithmetic the authority cannot survive. Chapter 2 is that arithmetic.

And then — because a door is only interesting if something lies beyond it — the rest of the book walks through. If a universe permits what this book calls apparent non-determinism, then agency becomes a quantity: a thing with an anatomy, a price list, thresholds, floors, and thieves. The remaining chapters measure it.

2

Part I. The Verdict and the Appeal · Chapter 2

The price of locality, in one chapter

In 1964, John Bell proved that three innocent-sounding assumptions cannot all survive contact with experiment. Stated plainly:

  1. Locality. Influence does not travel faster than light.
  2. Determinism. Outcomes are fixed by prior facts.
  3. Measurement independence. The experimenter’s choice of what to measure is statistically independent of the hidden facts of the thing measured — in slogan form: the universe does not rig your questions to fit its answers.

Experiments violate Bell’s inequalities. Therefore at least one assumption is false. Physicists mostly shop between abandoning the first (resulting in spooky action) and abandoning single outcomes altogether (resulting in many worlds). The third exit — that measurement independence fails, not by cosmic conspiracy but lawfully and partially — was long treated as the disreputable door. Then in 2010, Michael Hall asked the question that changes the register of the whole debate: if you take the third exit, what is the fare? And he answered it exactly, for the simplest case: to reproduce the quantum correlations of two entangled particles with a local, deterministic model, measurement independence must be relaxed by precisely (2−1)/3(\sqrt{2}-1)/3 — about 13.81%. Not all of it. Not none of it. That number.

A door with a posted price is a different object from a forbidden door.

Hall priced the two-particle case and one fragment of the three-particle case, and left the general problem open in 2011. It stayed open for fifteen years. The solution — the mathematics this book’s lineage rests on — computes the exact minimum relaxation for the full faithful statistics of the canonical multiparticle experiments, certified in exact arithmetic out to twenty-two particles, and finds the answers are not a mess but a law — stated there for every size, and since proven for every size [PROVEN / EXACT; the published record — arXiv:2608.00124, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21445609]:

F=R2(R+1),where R doubles with every second particle.F = \frac{R}{2(R+1)}, \qquad \text{where } R \text{ doubles with every second particle.}

One third at three particles. Two fifths at five. Four ninths at seven. 8/17, 16/33, 32/65 — a staircase, climbing with perfect regularity toward, and this is the theorem that matters most, a ceiling it can never reach: F≤1/2F \le 1/2, at every size, forever. The universe’s statistics never require measurement independence to be relaxed by more than half. Total determinism-by-conspiracy is never forced. The door is never welded.

The machinery, for those who want it

The staircase was the first paper. There is now a second [CONJECTURED SURFACE, certified exactly at the quantum point and at six rational points; the published record — arXiv:2608.18886], and Part V takes its exhibit from it. The original experiment that started all of this — two particles, two detectors — turns out to have not one posted price but two, on two different doors: how much measurement independence a local account must relax, and how efficient its detectors are permitted to be. The second paper computes the exact exchange rate between the two — relax less of one, pay more of the other, at a rate written down in closed form — exact to the digit where it has been certified, conjectured between — and then does something no result in this lineage had done before: it finds a specific, physical quantity that the standard experiment is mathematically incapable of seeing — checked only at the percent level through four decades of the most scrutinized experiments in physics, never below it, which is where the surviving accounts live — and it hands over a protocol that any well-equipped laboratory can run to measure it there. Whichever way that measurement comes out, a named family of accounts is bounded an order of magnitude tighter than the record now holds it. And one thing it cannot do, whichever way it comes out: touch the license. The ceiling above was proven by arithmetic over every strategy a local account could adopt; no coincidence count can raise it or lower it. The scan audits which ledger the surviving accounts pay in — never whether the door is open. (And to keep this book’s own fence intact: that exchange rate prices trade-offs within the surviving local accounts, between their two internal ledgers — never across the exits from Bell’s theorem, which remain unranked.) An exact price, an unmeasured column, an instrument anyone can pick up: the second half of this book uses all three.

Now, exactly what this result licenses and what it does not:

It does not prove you are free. A fully superdeterministic universe remains logically consistent. So does ordinary quantum mechanics with no hidden layer at all. The staircase takes no side.

The machinery, for those who want it

One argument, made by the author of the two papers and labeled as an argument, not a result. To compare exits at all, a common currency must be chosen — and here is a principled candidate: score each exit’s extrapolation against the constraints every other science already answers to. Thermodynamics. Information theory. No privileged observer standing outside the universe. No effects preceding causes. Every other discipline must tell its story through that highly constrained lens; the exits from Bell’s theorem have historically enjoyed a free pass from it — perhaps precisely because this third exit went unpriced. Under that currency, the priced exit is the conservative one: no influence outrunning light, no unobservable proliferating worlds, no retrocausality — full congruence with the physics everything else already obeys. Under other currencies — dynamical parsimony, or the refusal of hidden variables altogether — other exits win, which is why physicists still disagree, and why this paragraph is an argument. There is a second candidate currency, worth naming with its own caveat attached: the capacity to be audited. The canonical forms of the other exits are built to agree with quantum mechanics everywhere, which makes them untestable against it by design — their falsifiable cousins exist, but purchase their testability by disagreeing with the record in territory already measured, where the record squeezes them. The exit priced in this book turned out to carry its testable content in a column no experiment had measured — congruent with everything ever recorded, and still auditable [the sequel, arXiv:2608.18886; the exhibit that closes Part V tells that story — the unmeasured quantity, the theorem that hid it, the protocol that measures it]. And it does more than survive there. The paper that priced the exit also built it — an explicit local mechanism, with no stochastic ingredient, that pays exactly the posted price — and both the price and the mechanism come with things an experiment can look for. The solved detection sector predicts a fringe in the total coincidence rate as the analyzers turn (the exhibit of Part V), in a quantity recorded for forty years at the percent level and never below it. And the mechanism itself leaves a fingerprint on the correlation curve every Bell experiment measures: a softening of its extremes — where the quantum curve reaches perfect agreement and perfect disagreement, the mechanism falls short by up to about a percent, concentrated between the Bell angles. Resolving the mechanism more finely shrinks that softening and moves it between the angles tested; at every resolution tried it keeps the same shape, and whether it survives to the continuum is a question the paper leaves open and says so. No other account on the record is all of these at once: local, deterministic, priced below total conspiracy at every size, built as an explicit mechanism, and specific about what an experiment should find — a softening in a curve every Bell experiment already records, and a fringe in a sum that quantum mechanics says is flat. And whichever way those experiments come out, the ceiling of this chapter stands: the scan decides which ledger the surviving accounts pay in, never whether the door is open. Under that currency too, the priced exit stands alone — and the same caveat applies: an argument, not a theorem. But the reader is entitled to notice which currencies the rest of science is already paying in.

It proves that no one can claim mathematics took the side against you. Anyone asserting that physics requires the fully rigged universe is now making a claim with an exact counter-theorem. The sealed verdict — its authority borrowed from proofs that turn out not to lend it — is vacated on appeal. What remains is, just, like, your opinion, man — and you are free to decline opinions.

Hold on to the shape of what just happened, because the entire book repeats it at larger scales. A question that sounded metaphysical (am I free?) was converted into a question with units (what is the minimum price of pretending otherwise?), and the answer came back bounded, exact, and universal. Freedom was not proven. Freedom was priced — and its price, in measurement independence, was capped at one half.

The next chapter names the thing on the far side of the door — apparent non-determinism — and states exactly what the physics contributes to it (a license, never a number) before the measuring begins.

3

Part I. The Verdict and the Appeal · Chapter 3

Apparent non-determinism: the claim, precisely

Every framework has one chapter where a careless sentence would poison all the others. This is that chapter, so it will be short and it will be exact.

The thing on the far side of the door needs a name that does not smuggle in a conclusion. Free will is a courtroom of a phrase — two thousand years of theology and neuroscience shouting in it. This book uses a cooler term: apparent non-determinism, AND for short, and in mathematics the symbol δA\delta_A. Here is what it means, in one breath: an entity exhibits AND to the degree that its actions cannot be predicted from its local circumstances. A rock exhibits none — give the slope and the rain, and the rock is given. A person may exhibit a great deal — or, under certain conditions this book will price with uncomfortable precision, almost none.

Note what the definition does not mention: souls, quantum mechanics, consciousness, or the truth about determinism. AND is apparent — defined relative to what an observer can predict — which is exactly what makes it measurable, and measurability is the entire premise.

Now the sentence that must be said with total clarity, because every hostile reader arrives with its refutation pre-loaded, aimed at a claim this book does not make:

The physics of Chapter 2 contributes a license, never a number.

The staircase does not cause your Tuesday. The ceiling F≤1/2F \le 1/2 does not govern wages, and 8/17 at nine particles implies nothing about nine senators. Anyone who tells you this book derives economics from quantum mechanics has not read this paragraph, and you may return them to it. What the physics contributes is one thing, and it is not small: it guarantees the possibility class is open. Before Chapter 2, “agents whose actions are partly independent of circumstance” was a hypothesis a determinist could dismiss with borrowed authority. After Chapter 2, it is a standing possibility of the universe, priced and bounded, that no one can strike from the table. Everything measured in the rest of this book lives on that table — and lives or dies by its own evidence, in its own units, exactly as the survival of chemistry does not depend on re-proving atoms in every reaction.

One question remains before the measuring starts: why did settling the physics matter, if the numbers never transfer? Because of what the alternative licenses. If agents were rocks to every possible observer — if the universe published a complete state from which every action followed — then nothing could be stolen from them, and the theft this book prices would be a category error, like robbing gravity. The license says no such publication is forced. The ledger itself is narrower than the license and survives either way: it is defined in a seat, from what an observer with incomplete information can predict (Part III), and a deterministic agent with private knowledge scores on it exactly as a stochastic one does. What the license removes is the dismissal — that the whole ledger is about nothing. It converts every coercion from a neutral arrangement of matter into a possible taking, and possible takings can be measured, audited, and charged for. That conversion is the door. The rest of the book walks through it.

Part II. One Agent: The Anatomy of Freedom · Chapter 4

The Leaf and the Timetable

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

The two axioms say what this book assumes. One further decision, made in this chapter, says how it measures — and everything measured afterward stands on it: freedom needs two rulers, not one.

The obvious single ruler — call it unpredictability — asks: after seeing someone’s circumstances, how much doubt remains about what they will do? It sounds right. It is measurable. And it fails, in a way so instructive that the failure became the foundation. Because two very different things score high on unpredictability: a person steering their own life, and a dropped leaf tumbling in the wind. And two very different things score low: a coerced person, and a competent one in a world where the right move is obvious.

So this chapter splits the measurement in two. The first ruler, independence, keeps the old question: how little do circumstances predict your actions? The second, aim, asks the question the leaf fails: how much do your actions have to do with what actually comes next? Freedom, as this book will use the word from here on, means scoring on both rulers at once — and the entire book is a map of what that double score costs, who pays it, and who takes it.

§2The story: the harbor

Stand on a harbor wall in a stiff wind and watch three people.

The ferry captain runs the posted schedule. Weather within limits, she sails at the top of the hour to the island and back, the same crossing she has made four thousand times. And note something easily missed: she is never wrong. Her seamanship is real and her crossings are flawless. But anyone holding the timetable and a weather report can predict her whole day without watching her once. Her poverty is not error. It is that everything she does was already written in her circumstances.

The lost tourist is her opposite. He has no destination, no map he trusts, and he wanders the quays turning wherever the crowd or a smell or a seagull suggests. Nobody can predict his next turn — not you, and not really him. By the single ruler, he is the freest person on the harbor. And he is going nowhere. His unpredictability is genuine, and it serves nothing.

Then the sailor casts off — heading upwind. Watch him closely, because his behavior is strange by both of the other standards. He does not do what the wind says: he tacks, cutting angles the gusts never dictated, sometimes turning toward rough water. An observer reading only the wind and the harbor cannot call his moves. But neither is he wandering: every strange angle serves the same unwavering destination, and he arrives. The wind pushed everyone on that water today; the captain’s route was written by it and the timetable, the tourist scattered on it, and the sailor used it — visible in his wake as the only track that disagreed with the wind and still ended at the chosen port.

Independence without aim is the tourist. Aim without independence is the captain. The sailor is what the two rulers, together, are built to find.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Three results fence the space the two rulers draw. Stated here in words; formally in §4; proofs in the theorem file.

Theorem 1 The sage ceiling — Axiom 1, made quantitative PROVEN

Even a perfect agent — complete knowledge of its own future, unlimited deliberation — cannot reach total independence. Its remaining predictability equals exactly what its environment already knew about that future. You can never rationally be less predictable than your world is informative; ignoring a genuinely telling circumstance is not freedom but error. Every environment posts a ceiling, and the ceiling belongs to the environment. Cybernetics reached a neighboring sentence fifty years earlier — Conant and Ashby’s good-regulator theorem (1970), that every competent regulator must carry a model of what it regulates — and Theorem 1 is in its spirit: the sage’s predictability is the model it cannot help carrying. The difference is the quantity measured. Conant and Ashby bound the regulator’s structure; Theorem 1 prices its independence.

Theorem 2 Complementarity PROVEN

The environment’s information about the future is a fixed pot, split exactly two ways: it is simultaneously the ceiling on the captain’s aim and the floor under the sailor’s predictability. One quantity, two debts. (The partition above is a statement about information specifically; if aim is scored by raw success rate instead, the two quantities no longer sum to one — the audit is printed in §5.)

Proposition 3 Starved is not free PROVEN

Strip an agent of deliberation and its unpredictability rises — toward the leaf. On the single ruler, the most deprived agent scores as the most free. This inversion is why the single ruler is not merely imprecise but dangerous, and Chapter 7 will show it is exploitable.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

The two rulers, built from plain parts.

Doubt is counted in bits. One bit is one fair coin-flip of remaining uncertainty; three bits, three coin-flips. The standard name for counted doubt is entropy, written HH.

Ruler one — independence. Let AA be the action taken and EE the circumstances an observer sees. H(A∣E)H(A \mid E) counts the observer’s remaining doubt about AA after seeing EE. Scale it by the doubt a total stranger would have (log2\log_2 of the number of possible actions) and it lands on a 0-to-1 dial:

δA=H(A∣E)log2|A|\delta_A = \frac{H(A \mid E)}{\log_2 |A|}

δA=0\delta_A = 0: the captain — circumstances leave no doubt. δA=1\delta_A = 1: the tourist — circumstances say nothing.

Ruler two — aim. Let FF be the future the agent is steering toward — a state of the world the action is a bet on (where the fish are, what the weather does, what the market will come to want), never an outcome the action itself produces. FF is exogenous to AA everywhere in this book; what that rules out, and why the audit of Chapter 13 needs it, is said there. One more thing aim is not: a success rate. Information is blind to relabeling — an agent who always does the opposite of what the future calls for tracks it perfectly and fails every time — so aim measures the capacity to track the future, not whether the tracking was used well. The theorems of this book are about that capacity; a success score adds a decoding the rulers do not see. For the agents of this book the two move together, because every agent here is built to seek reward and so decodes in its own favor — the perverse case is an agent who knows the future and chooses to lose. Where the book prices a loss of aim as a loss, that is the agent it has in mind. The information the action carries about that future — written I(A;F)I(A;F), the number of bits of doubt about FF that watching AA removes — measures whether behavior is about anything. Scaled the same way:

aim=I(A;F)H(F)\text{aim} = \frac{I(A;F)}{H(F)}

The tourist: δA=1\delta_A = 1, aim =0= 0. The captain in fair weather: δA=0\delta_A = 0, aim =1= 1. The sailor lives where both are high — and Theorems 1 and 2 say exactly how high both can simultaneously be.

Theorem 1, formally. For an agent with full knowledge of FF and ample deliberation, the acted policy is A=FA = F, so H(A∣E)=H(F∣E)H(A \mid E) = H(F \mid E), and

δA(sage)=H(F∣E)log2|A|.\delta_A(\text{sage}) = \frac{H(F \mid E)}{\log_2 |A|}\,.

The sage’s ceiling is the environment’s ignorance of the future — one line, once the definitions exist. Theorem 2 follows by splitting H(F)=H(F∣E)+I(F;E)H(F) = H(F \mid E) + I(F;E): the second term is what the vane can capture (its aim ceiling) and the first is what the sage cannot shed (its predictability floor). The two debts sum to the whole pot.

§5The model, and its audits

The machinery, for those who want it

The world: a future FF with nn equally likely possibilities; an environment signal that reveals FF with probability 1−s1-s; a knowledge signal that reveals FF with probability ee; an agent acting on the exact Bayesian posterior, with deliberation controlled explicitly. All quantities computed by exact enumeration — no simulation, no fitted parameters. (The agent is the standard bounded-rational one — a Bayesian posterior sharpened by a single deliberation parameter, the form Ortega and Braun derived from information-processing costs in 2013 — so nothing in the engine’s driver is this book’s invention. What the book adds is the second ruler held up to a driver already standard in its field.)

Audits, as the opening pages promised. Theorem 1 was machine-checked on five hundred randomized worlds — arbitrary priors, arbitrary asymmetric channels — with worst-case error at the limit of computer arithmetic. Theorem 2 was checked the same way (no violations; equality exactly where the proof says) and additionally stress-tested at alphabet sizes up to 64. The complementarity identity is information-specific: re-run with raw success rate in place of I(A;F)I(A;F), the two quantities no longer sum to one, and no result in this book leans on the version that fails. Proposition 3 is an exact limit of the model class and was replicated under a second, independent model of deliberation in Chapter 7’s machinery — where the direction of the starved agent’s drift turns out to depend on what a mind falls back on when thought is taken, a fork with consequences of its own.

Part II. One Agent: The Anatomy of Freedom · Chapter 5

The Gate

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorem
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

Here is the finding of this chapter in one sentence: learning buys you no independence at all — none — until what you know beats what your surroundings already tell you; and the moment it does, independence arrives all at once.

The natural assumption — the one most readers will bring, because it was brought here first too — is the opposite: the comfortable belief that every bit of education makes a person a bit freer, smoothly, like filling a glass. The mathematics refused it. What it handed back instead was a threshold: a gate. Below the gate, education changes what you know but not what you do, because acting on weak knowledge against a clear world is simply a mistake, and rational people don’t make it. Above the gate, your own knowledge outranks the world, and your behavior stops being readable from your circumstances.

Education here means more than school. It is whatever leaves a person knowing something their surroundings do not announce: a class, a trade, an hour alone with a problem, years among the people they live with. The gate does not ask where the knowledge came from. It asks how often it is right.

One consequence deserves its own paragraph, because it runs against instinct. The clearer and more stable a person’s world, the higher their gate. Someone whose environment is orderly, legible, fully administered — where the “right” move is always obvious from the situation — needs more education before any of it purchases independence, not less. Order is not neutral. Order raises the bar.

§2The story: the intersection

Imagine learning to drive in a city where every intersection has a working traffic light. You are given driving lessons — theory, judgment, the physics of wet roads. Are you freer for it? Watch your actual behavior: at every light you do what the light says, exactly like every driver who never took your lessons. Your knowledge is real, but the world is so legible that following it is always the right call. Anyone watching the lights can predict you perfectly. Your lessons bought you nothing visible — yet.

Now the storm knocks the lights out. Suddenly the intersection says nothing, and the drivers split: most freeze or follow the car in front — still readable, now from each other. But the driver whose training finally exceeds what the intersection offers makes her own call — yield here, roll there — and for the first time, watching the intersection tells you nothing about her. Same driver, same lessons. The lessons crossed the gate only when the world stopped answering first. That is the whole theorem, lived: education pays nothing until it wins the argument with your surroundings — and a world of perfect traffic lights is a world where almost no one’s education ever wins.

One more turn at the same intersection. The lights are out and her training is good — but the two kinds of mistake are not priced alike. If she follows the car in front and it goes badly, she has a dented bumper and company. If she makes her own call and it goes badly, she loses the car, and with it the job the car gets her to. At those prices she follows the car in front, and she is right to. What decides it is not what she knows. It is what one mistake of her own would cost her, set against a mistake made in company: her mistake budget. The theorem below gives the number. In a world that is right half the time, lessons open the gate once they are right more than fifty times in a hundred. Let her own mistake cost ten times the shared one, and the same lessons must be right ninety-five times in a hundred before she acts on them. Her lessons did not get worse. The price of using them went up.

§3The theorem

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

Theorem 5 Activation threshold

In the model of §5, with environment reliability 1−s1-s and education fidelity ee, a rational agent’s independence δA\delta_A is exactly zero whenever e<1−se < 1-s, and strictly positive whenever e>1−se > 1-s. The gate sits at

e*=1−se^{\ast} = 1 - s

and its location does not depend on how finely the future is divided (proven and verified for every alphabet size tested, 4 through 64). PROVEN

Below the gate, the agent’s behavior has a name in economics: an informational cascade (Banerjee 1992; Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch 1992) — the rational discarding of a private signal when the public one is more reliable. Cascade theory studies the sequence of such decisions and how fragile it is. Theorem 5 is in its spirit and asks a different question: where the threshold sits, as a race between two reliabilities — and finds the answer indifferent to how finely the future is divided.

In words: education fidelity plus environmental noise must exceed one. Your knowledge and your world are in a reliability race, and only the winner steers you.

Theorem 5b The mistake-budget gate EXACT

The gate above assumed a mistake costs the same whichever way you make it. Let a self-directed mistake cost κ\kappa times a conformist one — the arithmetic of living without a buffer, where one wrong bet of your own means eviction — and the gate moves to

e*(κ)1−e*(κ)=κ(1−s)s+(κ−1)(1−1n),\frac{e^{\ast}(\kappa)}{1 - e^{\ast}(\kappa)} \;=\; \frac{\kappa(1-s)}{s} + (\kappa - 1)\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right),

recovering e*=1−se^{\ast} = 1-s exactly at κ=1\kappa = 1 and rising with κ\kappa. The second term is the case where both sources are wrong — paid once by the conformist, κ\kappa times by the self-directed — and it keeps the number of options in the formula: more ways to be wrong, a higher gate. At κ=10\kappa = 10 in a half-noisy world, the gate sits at 0.936 with two options, 0.947 with eight, and under 0.95 with any number: near-perfect knowledge required before independence is rational. The consequence deserves plain statement: a person can stand well above the education gate and remain rationally conformist — for want of a mistake budget. Environments that permit mistakes are not a kindness; they are a precondition. And a mistake budget, like time, is a resource that can be taken: a zero-buffer life is a welded gate wearing different clothes. The gate assumes the agent knows its own reliability. With noisy self-knowledge, the mistake ratio that maximizes a population’s per-decision accuracy is one where the population sits at its gate; below one where most sit above it (a margin silences people who should act); and without bound where most sit below it and do not know it — there, the accuracy-optimal rule is that nobody acts on their own judgment. That last case is the shared-tutor town of Chapter 11: the most accurate town per decision, and the one that starves. Accuracy and survival part company exactly there, which is why Chapter 14’s first rule — past the gate — comes before its others, and why the κ\kappa a zero-buffer life actually imposes, around ten, is justified by neither objective. (Who gets to buy mistake budgets back, and at whose expense, is Chapter 13’s business. Organizations have long had words near this one — slack, in Cyert and March’s behavioral theory of the firm (1963); psychological safety, in Edmondson’s study of teams (1999) — and the mistake budget is in their spirit while being a sharper object: a ratio, κ\kappa, that moves a proven gate by a computable amount.)

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it

Two quantities, built from plain parts.

Independence, δA\delta_A, asks: after seeing your circumstances, how uncertain does an observer remain about your action? Uncertainty is measured in bits — one bit is one fair coin-flip of doubt. If your circumstances pin your action completely, the observer holds zero bits of doubt: δA=0\delta_A = 0, the rock. If circumstances say nothing about your action, doubt is maximal: δA=1\delta_A = 1. (Formally: δA=H(A∣E)/log2|A|\delta_A = H(A \mid E)/\log_2 |A|, the conditional entropy of action given environment, scaled to [0,1][0,1].)

The gate, derived. Your environment EE points at your future correctly with probability (1−s)+s/n(1-s) + s/n — right most of the time, uniformly confused otherwise. Your education KK points correctly with probability e+(1−e)/ne + (1-e)/n. When the two disagree, a rational agent asks: which source is more likely to be right, given exactly this disagreement? Bayes’ rule makes it a ratio of the two channels’ odds:

follow K⇔e+(1−e)/n(1−e)/n>(1−s)+s/ns/n⇔ne1−e>n(1−s)s⇔es>(1−s)(1−e)⇔e+s>1.\begin{aligned}\text{follow } K \;&\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{e + (1-e)/n}{(1-e)/n} \;>\; \frac{(1-s) + s/n}{s/n}\\&\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{n\,e}{1-e} \;>\; \frac{n\,(1-s)}{s}\\&\Longleftrightarrow\; e\,s > (1-s)(1-e)\\&\Longleftrightarrow\; e + s > 1.\end{aligned}

Four lines. Notice the alphabet size nn cancels — the gate does not care how complicated the future is, only who is more reliable about it. Below the gate the agent follows EE everywhere (δA=0\delta_A = 0 identically); above it, the agent defects to its own knowledge wherever the two disagree, and δA\delta_A jumps.

The mistake-budget gate, derived the same way. On a disagreement the posterior’s weights on the environment’s future, on knowledge’s, and on neither stand in the proportion 1+n(1−s)/s1 + n(1-s)/s to 1+ne/(1−e)1 + n\,e/(1-e) to n−2n - 2. Acting with the environment costs 1 when it is wrong; acting on knowledge, κ\kappa:

follow K⇔κ[1+n(1−s)s+n−2]<1+ne1−e+n−2⇔e1−e>κ(1−s)s+(κ−1)(1−1n).\begin{aligned}\text{follow } K \;&\Longleftrightarrow\; \kappa\left[1 + \frac{n\,(1-s)}{s} + n - 2\right] \;<\; 1 + \frac{n\,e}{1-e} + n - 2\\&\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{e}{1-e} \;>\; \frac{\kappa(1-s)}{s} + (\kappa - 1)\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right).\end{aligned}

Theorem 5c The gate for any environment PROVEN

Drop the symmetry. Let the environment be any channel at all, and for a given signal let qmaxq_{\max} be the posterior weight it puts on its favorite future and qkq_k the weight it puts on the future the agent’s own knowledge names. The same four lines give the gate for that signal and that disagreement:

e*=qmax−qkqmax+(n−1)qk,e^{\ast} = \frac{q_{\max} - q_k}{q_{\max} + (n-1)\,q_k},

which is 1−s1-s in the symmetric world and in general a threshold per signal — a surface, not a number — with the same knife-edge character everywhere: below it the agent follows the environment; above it the agent defects. Checked against 215,000 Bayesian decisions on random channels with zero disagreements. Chapter 15’s “gate, generalized” is closed by this line; what the symmetric world hid was only that the threshold depends on how confidently the environment is pointing.

Two audits, because this book audits itself. The gate was re-derived under a deliberately hostile redefinition of “buys nothing” (requiring substantial, not merely nonzero, independence): the location moved by less than one part in a thousand. And the smooth-education belief was hunted across thousands of randomized worlds before its death was accepted: the threshold appeared in every one. EXACT

§5The model

The machinery, for those who want it

Everything above was computed in the simplest world that contains the question. A future FF: one of nn possibilities, all equally likely. An environment signal EE: reveals FF with probability 1−s1-s, otherwise says something uniformly random. An education signal KK: reveals FF with probability ee, otherwise uniformly random, independent of EE given FF. (Where the education was acquired does not enter; only how often it is right.) The agent sees both signals, computes the exact Bayesian posterior over FF, and acts on it (hurried agents were also computed via a softmax deliberation parameter; the gate result quoted here is for ample deliberation). Every number is exact enumeration over all cases — no simulation, no sampling, no fitted parameters anywhere.

What the small world does and does not license: the location formula e*=1−se^{\ast} = 1-s is proven in this class; the existence and knife-edge character of the gate, per decision, survived every generalization tried — alphabet sizes to 64, asymmetric randomized channels, hostile redefinitions. One thing does not travel, and Theorem 5c says why: on a channel whose signals point with different confidence, each decision has its own threshold, and a population’s activation against education is a staircase of small steps rather than one cliff — the sharp aggregate dead zone is a feature of worlds where every signal is equally reliable. Constants are class properties; the per-decision gate is not; the aggregate cliff is.

§6The code

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing
  • code/verify_theorems.py — the conjecture hunt that killed smooth education and exposed the threshold (runs in seconds).
  • code/delta_A_v1.py — the two-axis landscape where the dead zone is first visible as the black region below the diagonal.
  • code/dichotomy_scaling_and_audits.py — the gate at n=16,32,64n = 16, 32, 64: zero below, ~0.93–0.95 above, at the predicted location every time.
  • code/mistake_budget_T18.py — Theorem 5b in 196 worlds.
  • Theorem 5’s formal statement and proof: docs/THEOREMS_v1.md. Reproduction: Python 3, numpy. No further dependencies.

Part II. One Agent: The Anatomy of Freedom · Chapter 6

The Frontier, and the Plateau

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

Chapter 4 gave freedom two rulers: independence — how little your circumstances predict you — and aim — how much your actions serve where you’re going. This chapter asks the natural next question: how well can anyone score on both at once? Score everyone in the world on the two rulers and plot them as points: somewhere out there is an outer edge, the best simultaneous scores possible. That edge is called the frontier, and this chapter maps it.

Two findings. First, the frontier has a hard trade built into it: past a certain point, every further unit of aim must be paid for in visibility — being more effective makes you more readable, at an exact exchange rate. Second — and this is proven to exist, exactly — there is a region whose existence is easy to doubt and no longer possible to deny: agents who are perfectly unreadable, circumstances predicting nothing about them at all, whose actions nonetheless carry real information about the future they are steering toward. Not much; the region is narrow. But total unreadability, with genuine aim inside it, is possible. This region is the plateau, and the character who lives there is easiest to meet at a card table.

§2The story: the card player

Watch a poker player — call her Ines — from the seat of someone trying to read her.

A beginner is an open book: strong hand, big bet; weak hand, fold. Read the bets, read the hand. The obvious fix — the one every beginner is taught — is to mix it up: bluff sometimes, bet at random now and then. That helps, but a patient observer still finds the pattern, because “random now and then” still leans with the hand.

Ines does something stricter. She decides in advance what her betting should look like from the outside — how often a raise, how often a call, how often a fold — and she makes that outward pattern identical whatever the table shows. Strong board or weak, early or late: over her nights, her bets in any one visible situation are spread exactly as they are in every other. To pull this off, when her cards would push her one way more often than the pattern allows, she uses chance — a private die — to pull her bets back until the outward pattern is restored. Her randomness is not decoration on her decisions; it is shaped against what the table shows, deliberately, so that nothing the table shows predicts her. An observer with perfect records of every visible card she ever sat behind can call her next bet exactly as well as someone who never watched at all. What a bet says once it is made is another matter: it carries a little about the hand behind it, and that little is her winnings. The table can learn from her bet. It can never see the bet coming.

Here is the strange part, and the theorem of this chapter: Ines still wins. Not much — the discipline is expensive, because most of her bets are spent maintaining the disguise rather than pressing her advantages. But provably, exactly, more than chance — not more than the captain who simply follows the table’s tells, unless those tells are noise more than half the time; the plateau’s claim is information at zero readability, not the best hand in the room. Perfect unreadability and real winnings, together. That is the plateau.

And the plateau has an edge. If Ines wants to win bigger, she must start pressing her good hands harder than her pattern allows — and every extra dollar of expected winnings costs her a measurable amount of readability. Tells are not a weakness of bad players. Past the plateau, tells are the price of winning, posted by mathematics, and no skill at any level makes the price go away.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Theorem 6 The plateau PROVEN; edge OPEN

There exist strategies with perfect independence — δA=1\delta_A = 1 exactly, circumstances predicting nothing — and strictly positive aim. The plateau extends at least to c0c_0 — the aim of an agent who acts on the future exactly as often as the world is wrong — and its exact edge is open; beyond the edge, every additional unit of aim must be purchased with visibility. Full unreadability is never impossible; full aim is never unreadable (Theorem 1’s ceiling closes the far end). The trade is two-sided and exact.

A second refuted claim, kept. REFUTED — kept The first printing of this theorem put the plateau’s edge at the end of Ines’s simplest strategy — follow the target a fraction λ\lambda of the time, compensate the rest — and called that edge c0c_0: about five percent of full aim in the reference world. It was the edge of that strategy, not of the plateau. A later attack, mounted from a different direction — searching the hidden strategies directly, as vertices of the set they live in, rather than by gradient — found a strategy five times further out: act on the future whenever the world is wrong; scatter whenever it is right. Its aim has a closed form, printed in §4 — the aim of someone who follows the future exactly as often as the environment errs — and an asymmetric cousin goes further still. The plateau was five times wider than its first estimate held. The old number is kept because the belief that produced it — that hidden competence must be modest — is the natural one, and it is wrong.

Cryptographers hold the twin of this theorem under another name. Cachin’s model of steganography (1998) asks how much hidden payload a message can carry while its visible statistics remain perfectly those of innocent cover text — and the plateau is that perfect-security case, with aim as the payload, the uniform action as the cover, and the whitening residual as the embedding. On this model class Theorem 6 is not merely in the spirit of steganographic capacity; it is that quantity. That is the strongest thing the book can say about any of its parts: the same arithmetic stands in another field, proved for another purpose, and agrees.

A refuted conjecture, kept. REFUTED — kept The natural first belief — likely the reader’s as well — was that the frontier’s best strategies were the simple ones — act on your knowledge some fraction of the time, plain chance the rest. An optimizer owing no loyalty to elegance found strategies strictly better. Chasing why produced Theorem 6: the better strategies were Ines’s kind — chance shaped against the visible world, not sprinkled on top of it. The dead conjecture was the price of the plateau’s discovery, and both are printed.

A sign worth remembering. The plateau widens as the environment grows noisier: c0c_0 rises with the chaos of the world. Storms are the friend of whoever does not wish to be read. This sentence returns, at the scale of a whole town, in Chapter 11.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it

The frontier, precisely: among all strategies available to an agent, the set of best simultaneous scores —

frontier=the maximal achievable pairs (aim,δA).\text{frontier} = \text{the maximal achievable pairs } (\text{aim}, \delta_A).

Ines’s construction, in the model’s terms. The agent knows its target FF and sees its circumstances EE. It follows FF with a fixed probability λ\lambda, and with probability 1−λ1-\lambda draws its action from a compensating distribution rEr_E — chosen, for each circumstance EE, so that the overall action pattern given EE is exactly uniform: every action equally likely from the observer’s seat. Such a compensation exists whenever λ\lambda is small enough; the exact limit is

λ*=1n(1−s)+s\lambda^{\ast} = \frac{1}{n(1-s) + s}

where nn is the number of options and 1−s1-s the environment’s reliability. Up to λ*\lambda^{\ast}, δA=1\delta_A = 1 identically while aim grows with λ\lambda. Past λ*\lambda^{\ast}, this compensation is arithmetically impossible — the agent’s pull toward FF exceeds what any redistribution can hide. But the plateau does not end there; a different construction continues it. Let the agent act on FF exactly when the environment is wrong (F≠EF \ne E), and when the environment is right, scatter: the environment’s own answer with probability qq, each other action with the remainder spread evenly. Choosing qq so the action pattern given EE is exactly uniform gives q=λ*q = \lambda^{\ast} — the same constant — and δA=1\delta_A = 1 exactly with aim

c0=1−hn(s+(1−s)/n)log2n,c_0 = 1 - \frac{h_n\left(s + (1-s)/n\right)}{\log_2 n}\,,

where hn(m)h_n(m) is the entropy of a row whose favored entry has probability mm. Read it as a sentence: the hidden agent’s aim at the plateau is the aim of someone who follows the future exactly as often as the world is wrong. (In the reference world, 0.247 against the first printing’s 0.052; equivalently, c0c_0 at noise ss equals one minus the sage’s independence at noise 1−s1-s.) The edge itself lies further out, and the reason the first searches missed it is now understood: at perfect unreadability the action pattern is pinned, so the edge is the minimum of a concave function over a polytope — it sits at a vertex, where smooth optimizers never look. Searching vertices directly finds strategies at 0.335 in the reference world (0.311 at four options) — a third of full aim with no readability at all — so c0c_0 is an exact lower bound, the vertex search a numerical one, and the exact edge is open (Chapter 15) — except at three options, where it is closed at 1−1/log23≈0.3691 - 1/\log_2 3 \approx 0.369, and at four, where the best strategy found, (5log25+9log23−6)/64≈0.3105(5\log_2 5 + 9\log_2 3 - 6)/64 \approx 0.3105, is certified to lie within 0.0002 of the edge. The edge is not monotone in the number of options: lower at four than at three, and higher again at five and at six. Past the edge, readability begins, which is the posted price of §2.

Note the ceiling formula’s role: at full aim, Theorem 1 fixes δA=H(F∣E)/log2|A|<1\delta_A = H(F \mid E)/\log_2 |A| < 1. The frontier therefore runs from the plateau’s right edge (aim ≥c0\ge c_0, δA=1\delta_A = 1) down to the sage point (aim =1= 1, δA=\delta_A = the ceiling), and the exchange rate along the way is the price of aim in visibility.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

Same world as Chapter 4; strategies unrestricted. What is proven: the plateau’s existence; a closed-form lower bound c0c_0 on its edge, reached by an explicit strategy; and the two-sided trade. What is open: the plateau’s exact edge beyond four options, and the frontier’s exact shape from that edge to the sage point. An earlier printing of this section claimed the best curve then known was within a part in a thousand of the frontier. That was wrong near perfect unreadability — by a factor of five — and the correction is kept in §3, with the reason the first attack missed it: a search by gradient over a smooth parametrization does not find strategies that live at the corners of the feasible set; a search over the corners does. Both the gap and the lesson are handed to the reader in Chapter 15. The frontier was then re-attacked with the method that found the corpse — fix the visible pattern of choices, search the strategies consistent with it at their corners — and every point it returns is an exact strategy, hence a certified floor under the true frontier: aim at least 1.00 at δA=0.75\delta_A = 0.75; 0.86 at δA=0.80\delta_A = 0.80; 0.70 at δA=0.85\delta_A = 0.85; 0.53 at δA=0.93\delta_A = 0.93; 0.37 at δA=0.98\delta_A = 0.98; 0.35 at δA=0.99\delta_A = 0.99; 0.29 at δA=0.997\delta_A = 0.997; 0.28 at δA=1.00\delta_A = 1.00. The first printing’s curve lies below every one of these on the hidden side of the sage point. The figure is redrawn accordingly (figures/ the_plane_and_frontier_v2.png), with the plateau’s edge marked open. The plateau-widening sign (c0c_0 rising with environmental noise) survives the correction and strengthens — 0.10, 0.25, 0.46 as the world’s noise rises through 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 in the reference world; constants, as always, travel only with their class.

§6The code

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing
  • code/frontier_attack.py — the optimizer that killed the simple- strategy conjecture and the compensating construction that replaced it. (Its near-optimality claim is the second kept corpse.)
  • code/plateau_edge_T6prime.py — the construction that widened the plateau, its closed form, and the search that found the asymmetric strategies beyond it.
  • code/rig/plateau_edge_vertex_search.py — the edge as concave minimization over a polytope; successive linearization from random vertices; 0.335 at (6, 0.5), 0.311 at (4, 0.5).
  • code/rig/plateau_edge_bnb.py — certified ceilings by branch-and-bound: the three-option edge closed, the four-option edge fenced.
  • code/frontier_polytope_attack.py — the re-attack of the frontier by fixed choice pattern; every output point is an exact strategy.
  • code/figure_plane_and_frontier_v2.py — the redrawn figure.
  • code/plateau_hit_rate_bound.py — how often a hidden agent can be right, against the captain: more only when noise passes one half.
  • code/delta_A_v1.py — the two-ruler landscape on which the plateau first appeared.
  • Formal statements, the refutation record, and proofs: docs/THEOREMS_v1.md.

Part II. One Agent: The Anatomy of Freedom · Chapter 7

Cheap Theft

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

This is the chapter where the book’s title comes due — the price list itself. So it begins by keeping the promise of the front matter: theft, defined before the word does any work.

An agent holds a position on the two rulers of Chapter 4, and its resources — knowledge, time, privacy, the stability of its own hours, the means to survive a mistake — determine the best positions available to it: the frontier of Chapter 6 — computed always at the system’s current capacity, not at nature’s. (The relevant baseline for a worker at the Harbor Grill is what the modern world’s accumulated stability makes possible now, not what a famine-stalked ancestor endured; a defense of theft that appeals to the stone age has conceded the modern ledger.) Theft is displacement by taking: any act by another party that pushes an agent off its frontier, or pushes the frontier itself inward, by taking or degrading one of the agent’s own resources — so that no position the agent could reach improves, and at least one gets worse. That is the entire definition. It names no villain. It is the same kind of statement as “the dent is three millimeters deep.” Whether a given displacement was justified, paid for, or consented to is a question for courts and philosophers. That it happened, and how large it was — those are now questions for arithmetic.

Two things the definition does not call theft, said now so the word stays sharp.

The first is a more legible world. A flawless neighbor (Chapter 10) or a working traffic light (Chapter 5) also moves the frontier — but by reshaping it: the independence ceiling falls while the competence available to anyone who follows rises. Nothing was taken; something was given. That is rivalry, priced in Chapter 10.

The second is a job that tells a person what to do. A script that must be followed leaves no room for a judgment of one’s own during the hours it covers — a surgeon’s checklist does exactly that, and robs no one. So the test is not run on the hours of the job. It is run on the whole life: the hours sold, and what the wage, the security and the remaining time make possible outside them. A scripted job that pays enough to steady the rest of a life widens that life’s frontier while it narrows the working day, and is not theft. A scripted job that also takes the time, the stability and the margin for error a person would need to do anything else narrows both, and is. The ledger keeps the working day and the life in separate columns — the task plane and the life plane — and calls theft only what shrinks the life.

The test has a second edge. A job can hand back every hour it promised and still take what those hours were for. Put a worker on a complaints line, with a script that forbids the one thing that would end each call: giving the caller what the caller is owed. The firm keeps what it did not concede. The cost of not conceding is paid by two people who are not on its books — the caller, in time, and the worker, who absorbs the caller’s anger for a shift and goes home with the evening whole on the clock and little left to spend in it. Hochschild named that work emotional labor (1983), and three decades of studies find that showing on script what one does not feel goes with exhaustion (Hülsheger and Schewe 2011, ninety-five studies). The ledger books that evening with the stolen hour, because the time gate of this chapter is counted in thought, not in clock time. The surgeon’s checklist and the complaints script both leave no room for judgment while they run. They differ twice: the checklist points the surgeon at what the patient needs and the script points the worker away from what the caller needs; and they differ in what is left of the worker when the shift ends.

Two rules about baselines, because a displacement is always from somewhere. First, every entry on the ledger is measured against a named feasible alternative — the worker without the job, the same job arranged differently — and the number changes with the baseline, so the baseline is printed with the number. Second, identifying a loss is not attributing it: that a worker’s capacity fell under a practice does not by itself say the practice caused the fall. Attribution needs the practice compared with its alternative, and Chapter 13 does it three ways: the same person followed across years, a city that changed its scheduling law beside cities that did not, and stores assigned to steadier schedules by lot.

And once theft has a size, it has a price list. This chapter computes it: for every resource an agent holds, the exact yield of taking some. The list has a headline, and it is the book’s darkest finding: the most efficient theft of freedom never makes its victim predictable — and never registers on the single ruler at all.

§2The story: the manager who steals nothing

The Harbor Grill has a manager who has never taken a thing. Every hour is paid to the cent. No till has ever come up short on his watch. Ask an auditor: nothing is missing.

What he takes is the shape of his workers’ time. The schedule posts Sunday night for a week that starts Monday. Shifts move on a day’s notice. Slow afternoon? Workers sent home mid-shift, unpaid for the hours that vanish. Busy evening? A text at four for a shift at six. No worker can plan a class, a second job, a doctor’s visit, a family dinner, or an hour of quiet thought more than a day ahead — every plan is written in pencil, and the eraser belongs to the manager. An auditor counting objects and dollars finds a clean ledger. (The manager will get his full say — the strongest defense his position affords — in Chapter 13.) What has been taken never appears on any inventory, because what has been taken is capacity: the ability to point one’s hours at anything of one’s own.

The mathematics says this theft leaves two kinds of victim, depending on what a person’s mind does when its planning time is taken away.

Nadia’s mind, overloaded, spins loose. Her days shatter into fragments; she starts things and abandons them, decides and un-decides. Watch her and you can predict nothing — on the single ruler, Nadia scores as remarkably free. What’s gone is her aim.

Tomas’s mind, equally overloaded, does the opposite: it hands the wheel to whatever is directly in front of him. The order screen, the line at the counter, the next text from the manager — each moment’s demand becomes his next act. He stays orderly, productive, even competent. On any dashboard he scores fine. What’s gone is everything about his day that his situation didn’t dictate.

Name the mechanism before the victims, because it is the chapter’s real subject: the schedule’s chaos was not created by the manager — it was relocated by him. Demand varies; that variance is a cost, and someone must absorb it. A business can absorb it on its own books — idle staff on slow days, overtime premiums on busy ones. Or it can transfer the variance onto its workers’ lives, where it destroys planning, aim, and δA\delta_A off any book anyone keeps. Call it what it is: stochasticity transfer — the moving of variance from a party who would have to account for it onto parties who cannot. (The manager believes he has answers to all of this — that the transfer was priced and agreed to — and his defense will be heard at full strength, and answered, in Chapter 13.) Economics has watched this happen at national scale and given it a name — Hacker’s great risk shift (2006): three decades of economic risk moving from institutions onto households. Stochasticity transfer is in that spirit and is the more general object — defined on any variance channel, inside a firm as readily as across an economy, and priced here by elasticity rather than described.

And an hour is not an hour. Thinking time has a gate of its own, twin to Chapter 5’s: until a person has had enough of it to out-think what the situation in front of them already makes obvious, more time buys nothing; just past that point it buys more than it ever will again; and from there each added hour buys less. So the hours that matter most are the first few past the gate — and those are the hours a moved shift takes from someone with few to spare. In this chapter’s model, an hour taken from the time-poor destroys about seventy times the agency of an hour taken from the time-rich, in proportion to what each has, and nearer two hundred times hour for hour. The Grill’s schedule does not take the same thing from everyone it touches.

Two workers, opposite symptoms — one scattered, one on autopilot; you know both, and may have been both — and neither was robbed, according to every measure that doesn’t use two rulers. That invisibility is not an accident. It is, this chapter proves, exactly why this theft is the cheap one.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Corollary 7.1 Cheap theft EXACT

Destroying an agent’s aim while leaving its unpredictability intact is vastly cheaper than making the agent readable — against agents of Ines’s kind (Chapter 6), cheaper by roughly a thousand to one, whatever the attacker wants. The single ruler cannot register the loss even in principle.

Theorem 10 The price list EXACT

Computed as elasticities — percentage of agency lost per percentage of resource taken, a form with no units and no assumptions about the attacker’s costs: (i) against unreadable agents, only aim can be attacked at all; (ii) agents near their education gate (Chapter 5) are the cheapest to unmake — a small theft of knowledge, or a small increase in how predictable their world is, drops them into the dead zone entirely, at yields ten times any other entry on the list (on the independence ruler; Chapter 10 prices what the second move gives back on the other); (iii) a stolen hour is not a stolen hour: taken from someone with few, its yield is roughly seventy times its yield against someone with many in proportional terms (the elasticities), and nearer two hundred times per unit of time taken.

Theorem 16 The two victims, and the time gate EXACT

Which victim the theft produces — Nadia or Tomas — depends only on what an overloaded mind falls back on: loose scatter, or the demand in front of it. Both routes destroy agency at full cheap-theft efficiency. And thinking time has a gate of its own, twin to Chapter 5’s: deliberation buys zero independence until accumulated thought outweighs what the situation already makes obvious — and then it activates all at once. The field has already measured the thing this gate formalizes: Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir and Zhao (2013) and Shah, Mullainathan and Shafir (2012) showed scarcity — of money, of time — taxing the deciding mind itself, not merely its options. The time gate is in the spirit of that finding and makes one claim it did not: that the tax arrives as a threshold, zero-then-jump, rather than a slope — which is exactly what the field audit of Chapter 15 can check. Placed inside the standard heterogeneous-agent macro model (Chapter 14 §5C), a threshold of the same kind is what makes a large monetary easing louder in output and quieter in balance sheets than any linear model of it reports — in the host where wages are sticky.

Proposition 8 Where an hour is worth most EXACT

Below the time gate, extra thinking time buys nothing. Just past the gate, it buys more than it ever will again. From there, each additional hour buys less than the one before. This is why clause (iii) lands where it does: the most valuable hours anyone owns are the first few past the gate — which are exactly the hours the time-poor lose first.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

Elasticity, built from plain parts: if taking 1% of a resource costs the victim 2% on an agency ruler, the elasticity is 2. It is a pure ratio — no dollars, no assumed prices — so the price list holds for any attacker, whatever their costs, because it ranks yields, not expenses.

The list’s dominant entries, from the computation: for agents on the plateau, every resource attack (time, knowledge of the world) moves the independence ruler by elasticity at most 0.009 while moving aim by 1.5 to 2.0 — the thousand-to-one of Corollary 7.1. Near the gate e*=1−se^{\ast} = 1-s of Chapter 5, the independence ruler’s elasticity against education spikes to about 9, and against the world’s predictability to about 4.5. And aim’s elasticity against time is 0.565 for a time-poor agent versus 0.008 for a time-rich one — the seventy of clause (iii). (Elasticities are proportional sensitivities; the return per unit of time, dQ/dt=εQ/tdQ/dt = \varepsilon\,Q/t, differs by about 190 between the same two agents, because the time-poor agent’s smaller budget is in the denominator. “An hour returned” means the per-unit number.)

The time gate, precisely: model thought as consulting your own knowledge in noisy steps, with the situation’s suggestion available for free. A single weak consultation loses the reliability race of Chapter 5 and is rationally ignored; independence stays at exactly zero until accumulated consultations outweigh the situation’s reliability, then jumps. The same inequality as the education gate — e+s>1e + s > 1 — with accumulated thought standing in for ee. One law, two currencies. Nothing in the model is clock time: it counts consultations. A person handed the same hours with fewer consultations left in them has been moved down the same curve as a person handed fewer hours.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

The price list was computed in the world of Chapters 4–6 by exact enumeration; elasticities are unit-free but, like every constant in this book, travel only with their model class — the seventy is real in its world, and Chapter 13 is where the world is audited.

The two victims required a modeling choice this book declines to make: what does an overloaded mind emit — loose scatter, or the demand in front of it? Both versions were built and run. Cheap theft holds in either. But an earlier result had to be narrowed by the comparison, and the narrowing is printed: the first printing reported that unreadable agents keep their unreadability when their time is stolen (only their aim dies). That is true if a rushed mind emits scatter — scatter is unreadable by nature. If instead a rushed mind does what the situation suggests, the opposite happens: the unreadable agent, out of time, becomes an open book. Which world a given person lives in is an empirical question about minds, not mathematics, so the book keeps both and labels each claim with the version it needs.

Nothing here requires the Harbor Grill’s manager to have read this book. Ordinary profit-seeking, ordinarily optimized — engagement tested, schedules tuned, churn tolerated — discovers these high-yield squares the way water discovers cracks. The list accuses no one of understanding it. It predicts where extraction, wherever it optimizes, will be found parked. Predictions can be checked.

  • code/iterative_time_T16.py — the time gate and the Tomas version; code/stealth_gates.py — the Nadia version.
  • code/delta_A_v1.py — Proposition 8’s shape, visible in the deliberation sweep.

Part III. Watchers: Freedom Is Relative to an Observer · Chapter 8

The Watchers

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

Every score in this book so far has carried a silent phrase, and this chapter makes it speak. Unreadable — to whom? Independence was defined as how little your circumstances predict you, but “your circumstances” are not one thing: they are whatever a particular watcher can see, and watchers see differently. Stated honestly, freedom is always freedom from someone’s seat: the same person, on the same day, holds a different independence score for every watcher in their life — and all of the scores are correct.

This is not a loophole in the framework. It is the framework refusing to let anyone say “free” without saying from whose sight. And taking that refusal seriously produced the strangest exact result in this book: there is a way of watching that makes the most unreadable person in the room the most readable one — without changing anything the person does.

§2The story: three seats, and the learned conviction

Theo is one man with three watchers.

His employer sees his schedule, his badge swipes, his output. From that seat, Theo is nearly a timetable: predictable to the minute, independence close to zero. His bank sees his purchases and payments — a different window, through which Theo is moderately readable: the rent repeats, the groceries cycle, but Tuesday’s detour is invisible. His neighbor sees comings and goings and nothing else; from her seat Theo is mostly mystery. Three watchers, three scores, one man, one day — and no one of the three is wrong. Ask “is Theo free?” and the honest answer is a question back: from which seat?

Now bring back Ines from Chapter 6 — the card player whose private die keeps her betting pattern identical whatever she holds — and seat a fourth kind of watcher behind her: one who can see the die itself. Here is the result that reverses the intuition: this watcher does not merely chip away at her disguise. From this seat, Ines is more readable than a beginner who never disguised anything — because her strategy was mostly careful machinery built around the die, and once the die is seen, the machinery is all that’s left, and machinery is legible. The discipline that made her the most unreadable player at the table makes her, under this one gaze, the most readable. It does not take much: seeing barely a third of her rolls already leaves her more exposed than the beginner.

And there is a second inhabitant of Ines’s territory, whose version of this story is quieter and worse. Elias plays no dice at all. He acts on a conviction — a private theory about how things really work, reaching past anything the table shows — and he acts on it consistently, not even certain himself that it’s true. To every ordinary watcher, Elias is indistinguishable from noise: his moves track something no visible circumstance contains. What looks like randomness is a hypothesis the watcher doesn’t hold. But note what this means: Elias has no die to hide. His entire unreadability is the privacy of one idea. The watcher who learns his theory doesn’t reduce him to a beginner — she reduces him to a wind-up toy, every future move written out in the one sentence she acquired. For Ines, surveillance had to watch a coin, roll after roll. For Elias, it only had to learn a conviction, once.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Theorem 9 Watchers, and the inversion EXACT

Independence is defined relative to a watcher’s information: δA(𝒪)\delta_A(\mathcal{O}) for a watcher who sees 𝒪\mathcal{O}. An agent of Ines’s kind is unreadable in full (δA=1\delta_A = 1) to a watcher who sees only circumstances — and, to a watcher who also sees her source of chance, readable below the 0.75 of a fully open, undisguised expert: at 0.29 for the strategy that follows the target a fixed fraction of the time and compensates the rest, and at 0.65 for the strategy that acts on the future where the world is wrong and scatters where it is right (Chapter 6 §4; same coin model). The crossover comes at roughly one third visibility of the source of chance for the first strategy and seven tenths for the second. Most of the second strategy’s unpredictability is the future itself, not a coin, and the future is the one thing a watcher who buys the coin still does not hold: chance spent where the world is wrong is chance the watcher cannot buy. Partial watching costs her linearly — every additional fraction of the die seen buys the watcher the same additional exposure.

Corollary Privacy is load-bearing EXACT

For unreadable agents, the price list of Chapter 7 contains exactly one entry that touches independence at all: visibility of their source of chance — or, for Elias’s kind, of their private hypothesis. Privacy is not a comfort of agency. It is the wall it stands on, and the only wall an attacker needs.

Theorem 9′ The sandwich: what a watcher who holds the coin can and cannot take PROVEN

For any agent whose action is a function of the future, her circumstances, and a private coin that does not know the future, a watcher who sees both circumstances and coin reads her between two walls:

I(A;F∣E)≤H(A∣E,R)≤H(F∣E).I(A;F \mid E) \;\le\; H(A \mid E, R) \;\le\; H(F \mid E).

Upper wall: no agent, once her coin is watched, is ever less readable than the open sage — Theorem 9’s inversion is not a property of Ines’s strategy but of every strategy, with equality only for agents whose actions are an invertible relabeling of the future. Lower wall: a watched agent keeps at least the future-information her actions carry beyond what circumstances already carry. The proof is three lines — the top because a function has no more uncertainty than its argument, the bottom because the coin, knowing nothing of the future, cannot subtract any of it — and it is the law behind the parenthetical above: Ines’s simplest strategy carries 0.09 of its independence as future and reads at 0.29; the strategy that spends its chance where the world is wrong carries 0.43 and reads at 0.65. A watcher who buys the coin can strip everything except the part of you that was tracking the future. That part is not for sale, because he does not hold the future either.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

The subscript, made explicit: for a watcher whose seat shows 𝒪\mathcal{O},

δA(𝒪)=H(A∣𝒪)log2|A|—\delta_A(\mathcal{O}) = \frac{H(A \mid \mathcal{O})}{\log_2 |A|} \;\;\text{---}

remaining doubt about the action, given everything that seat reveals. Theo’s three scores are this one formula at three values of 𝒪\mathcal{O}. All of Chapters 4–7 used 𝒪=\mathcal{O} = circumstances; nothing there changes — it acquires a label.

The inversion, by construction: Ines’s strategy is λ\lambda-follow-the-target plus compensation drawn from her die (Chapter 6, §4). Condition on the die: the compensation — most of her behavior, since λ≤λ*\lambda \le \lambda^{\ast} is small — becomes a fixed, known function; the only doubt left is the small λ\lambda-weighted thread that tracks her target, and that thread is partially pinned by circumstances too. Result: δA({circumstances, die})=0.29\delta_A(\{\text{circumstances, die}\}) = 0.29 in the model, versus 0.75 for the undisguised expert, whose behavior at least tracks a future the circumstances don’t fully reveal. For partial visibility — the die seen with probability ρ\rho — the score is exactly the straight line between the two endpoints, hence the early crossover at ρ≈1/3\rho \approx 1/3.

Elias, in the model’s terms: his conviction is a knowledge channel — information about the future carried by neither the circumstances nor any die. While private, it places him in Ines’s corner of the two-ruler plane (that corner was never about dice; it is about acting on what the watcher cannot see). Disclosed, his behavior is a deterministic function of known inputs: δA\delta_A collapses not to 0.29 but toward zero. Conviction buys deeper unreadability than chance, and pays more completely when the wall falls.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

Computed in the world of Chapters 4–6 by exact enumeration; the numbers 0.29, 0.75, and the one-third crossover are properties of that world and travel only with it. What is class-robust: the existence of the inversion, the linearity of partial watching, and the single-entry structure of the corollary. The “watcher” here is a bookkeeper — she conditions on what she sees and recomputes her odds; she does not yet learn over time from Ines’s history. Watchers with memory, and what an agent’s habits leak to them across weeks, are the next chapter’s machinery, and they sharpen this one’s moral considerably.

§6The code

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing

  • code/frontier_attack.py — the construction whose machinery the inversion exposes.
  • Formal statements and proofs: docs/THEOREMS_v1.md.
