Part III. Watchers: Freedom Is Relative to an Observer · Chapter 9

Habits and Coins

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

Chapter 8’s watchers held snapshots. This chapter gives them the thing real watchers have: memory. A watcher with memory turns your past into evidence against your future — every day you are observed, the file on you thickens, and yesterday’s you testifies about today’s. So the question sharpens from can you be unreadable? to the one that decides lives: can you stay unreadable, against someone who never stops learning you?

The answer has two parts. Part one: staying unreadable requires genuinely fresh choices, made daily — choices no record contains and no habit dictates. Count them the simplest way possible: in coin flips. A choice between two options that nothing in your past determines is one flip. Two flips can pick freely among four options; three flips, among eight. The question “how spontaneous are you?” becomes countable: how many honest flips go into each of your decisions?

Part two is the chapter’s finding, and it is stranger: how many flips you make matters less than what your flips are allowed to decide. Two people with identical habits and identical flips per day can differ totally in what a lifelong file extracts from them. In one arrangement, the file eventually wins no matter how many flips are made. In the other, a known and modest number of flips — enough to cover the day’s real options — makes the file, however thick, worth nothing at all.

§2The story: the courier’s two wirings

Vera is a courier who carries things worth stealing — cash payrolls, signed documents, small valuables. Her enemy is not the traffic; it is anyone who can predict her route, because a predictable courier can be waited for, and a courier who can be waited for gets robbed. Her adversary is patient and keeps a file: every route she has ever ridden, every departure time, every turn, for years. Vera has habits, as everyone does — districts she knows best, hours her body prefers, corners her hands take without asking. And she has her flips: each morning, a few honest coin flips’ worth of choices that nothing in her file determines.

The first wiring: flips decide the small things. Vera’s habits pick the frame of the day — which district, which window of hours — and her flips choose only within it: this alley or the next one, ten minutes early or late. It feels unpredictable, and for the first two weeks it is. Then the file catches the frame. Habits surface in any honest record, and once the robber knows the frame, her flips are a bird loose in a closed room — genuinely free, and only within walls he has already mapped. He does not need her alley — robbers do not ambush alleys; they wait at choke points. Knowing her district and her hour, he covers the one bridge in, and catches her at whatever alley she flips. (If his success required matching her exact alley, her inside-the-frame flips would protect her about seven days in eight — which is exactly why what matters is not how many flips you have, but which level of choice they rule.) Here is the bitter part: let this Vera flip more — twice as many flips, four times as many — and her safety barely moves. Flips that only decide details inside a habit-chosen frame are flips the file has already fenced in.

The second wiring: flips decide the big things. Same habits, same number of flips — different jurisdiction. Now the flips choose the frame itself. Her city has eight districts: three flips each morning pick the district — any district, every morning, all eight genuinely possible. Her habits still exist, but they are demoted to a lean: she still prefers the riverside, and the preference now only tilts the odds a little, the way a slightly bent coin still lands both ways. The file still learns her lean — the robber truly comes to know that she favors the riverside. And it buys him almost nothing, because the flips, not the preference, pick the district. Knowing how her coin is bent tells him how often she’ll ride the riverside across a year; it does not tell him where she’ll be today, and today is when a robbery has to happen.

Why “enough flips to cover the day’s real options” is the magic amount: one flip picks freely between 2, two flips among 4, three among 8. If Vera’s real choice each morning is among eight districts, three honest flips cover the menu — every option stays genuinely live every day, and the file’s knowledge of her leanings changes the long-run frequencies without ever pinning the day. Fewer flips than the menu needs, and gaps appear that habit fills — and habit is what the file owns. This is the exact sense of the chapter’s constant: in the model worlds, two to three flips per decision, given jurisdiction over the big choices, made perfect knowledge of an agent’s habits predict her no better than total ignorance — to the last decimal.

So the law of the chapter, plainly: a watcher with memory does not extract your flips. He extracts your wiring. If your habits decide the frame and your flips decide the details, the file wins — always, eventually, at any number of flips. If your flips decide the frame and your habits merely bend the coin, a modest number of honest flips beats the deepest file ever kept.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Theorem 11 The floor, and the two wirings [EXACT floors; watched decay verified by simulation with exact bookkeeping]

(i) Against a learning watcher, unreadability decays from its first-day value to a permanent floor — and the decay is fast: most of what a file will ever extract, it extracts in the first ten to twenty observations. First looks are the watcher’s version of first hours (Chapter 7): worth the most. (ii) Under the first wiring (flips decide the small things), the floor sits permanently below the exposure of someone who never disguised anything — Chapter 8’s inversion made chronic — at every coin size tested, for the strategy that follows the target a fixed fraction of the time (the margin on the wider plateau is Theorem 11′ (iii)). More coin does not raise a gated floor. (iii) Under the second wiring (flips decide the big things), the floor rises with the number of flips, and once the flips are enough to name a habit — three per decision, for this world’s eight habits — it reaches the first-day value exactly: the file becomes information-theoretically worthless. Perfect knowledge of Vera’s habits predicts her no better than ignorance. (iv) With no coin at all, both wirings are fully extractable.

Theorem 11′ The dichotomy, hardened EXACT; 3,372 wirings

(i) The one-time-pad point is set by the number of habits. Under the second wiring, perfect knowledge of the habit becomes worthless exactly when the fresh key is at least as long as the habit — h≥log2(number of habits)h \ge \log_2(\text{number of habits}). Three is log28\log_2 8, the model world’s habit count; a thousand habits need ten flips. (ii) The two wirings are the ends of one curve. Index a wiring by its reach — how far the fresh bits can travel across the choice space — and the floor depends on reach alone, is non-decreasing in it, and is identical across habit-space sizes at equal reach. A wiring drawn at random lands near the additive end: gating is something a routine has to do. (iii) The gated inversion is a margin, not a law. On the wider plateau — the strategy that spends its chance where the world is wrong — a habit-reader has little left to take, and the gated floor rises toward the open expert’s exposure: at four options in a half-noisy world it stays below by 0.07; in a six-option world that is mostly right it crosses above, 0.564 against 0.538. [REFUTED in one world of six; corpse kept.] (iv) The exception is a coarse-habit effect, and it vanishes. As the habit space refines, each habit’s cell on the quantile axis shrinks inside a single bin of every choice rule, the action becomes a function of the future given the habit, and the gated floor converges to one value for every number of fresh bits — the same value as with no fresh bits at all — which is at most the open expert’s exposure, H(F∣E)H(F \mid E), by the data-processing inequality, and strictly below it whenever the policy maps two futures to one action. [PROVEN; EXACT: at a thousand habits the gated floor varies by 0.0015 across hh in every world, and no gated floor sits above the sage at 64 habits or more anywhere in the sweep.] Fresh bits inside a wide cell can push a coarse habit’s floor over the ceiling; a fine habit’s cannot. The inversion is universal for fine habits, at every hh.

Theorem 20 The inversion costs no theory [EXACT floors; learned to three decimals in 72 of 72 worlds]

Any sufficiently flexible learner — a sequence model of under a million parameters never told that a habit exists, or a plain frequency table — reaches the exact seed-known floor within five to ten observations, the same day the perfect Bayesian does. The inversion of Theorems 9 and 11 is achieved by every such watcher, on every wiring tested, at habit spaces of eight and of a thousand. The habit space’s size does not protect: a thousand habits are read faster and further than eight, because finer habits make each action more determinate. The one watcher who reads above the floor is the one holding a confident wrong model of the wiring — who reads worse than ignorance in 52 of 72 worlds. The “strongest watcher” of Theorem 11 is the floor’s name, not its price.

Result R6 The pad is a race [SIMULATION; existence results]

Theorem 11(iv) says that with no coin both wirings are fully extractable. Let the coin instead be a generator — a deterministic rule with kk hidden bits whose outputs look fresh. The second wiring’s protection then lasts exactly as long as the watcher cannot acquire those kk bits within the watched lifetime. For a learner of under a million parameters watching 512 days: an 8-bit generator is a habit — the “worthless” file reads Vera at 0.34, below the gated floor, within a week; a 12-bit one is a habit within a season; a 16-bit one is half-read; a 32-bit one is still a coin. The watcher who assumes the coin is fresh never moves: that is the price of assuming freshness, and it is the whole gap. In the gated wiring, cracking the coin buys almost nothing — the coin was never doing the work there. One training run per world, and the generators are the weakest kind; what is established is that a watcher of this size can do it. A coin is a word about the watcher.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

Freshness, measured: h=h = honest flips per decision. The habits, measured: a persistent pattern the watcher can learn — in the model, a fixed personal offset drawn once and leaking slowly through behavior.

The two wirings, precisely. Gated: the flips select only within the habit’s cell — the learned offset chooses the region of the choice space, and the flips pick details inside it. Wide: the flips select over the whole choice space, and the offset only bends the odds among outcomes. The watcher runs honest bookkeeping — updating beliefs about the offset from every observed action, by the standard rules of evidence — and his remaining doubt about the next action is Vera’s score, day by day.

Wiring two’s endpoint has an ancestor cryptographers met in 1949 — the one-time pad, the unbreakable code whose key is as fresh as the message. The identity is the same: when the fresh key is as large as the choice itself and ranges over all of it, knowing the offset shifts which unpredictable thing happens but not how unpredictable it is — Shannon’s perfect-secrecy condition, restated for behavior. The gated wiring can never satisfy it, because its key is confined to a cell the watcher learns. The wiring dichotomy itself has an older ancestor in the same field: Kerckhoffs’s principle (1883), that a cipher must survive the enemy knowing everything but the key. Wiring one keeps its secret in the habit structure, which a watcher learns; wiring two keeps it in the fresh bits, which a watcher cannot. The book’s version is in that spirit and is tested rather than assumed — against a watcher who also sees outcomes.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

The floors — the permanent values — are exact enumeration. The decay curves toward them average many simulated watched lifetimes, each with exact belief-updates inside; with Theorem 20’s learned watchers and Result R6 they are this chapter’s simulation-assisted results, and are labeled accordingly. The specific constants (the one-third, the “three fresh choices”) are properties of the model world and travel only with it — the three is log28\log_2 8, as Theorem 11′ says. The dichotomy held its shape across every world size and channel tested on the strategy this chapter was written for. On the wider plateau found afterward it held at four options in a half-noisy world (gated floors rising to 0.62–0.70 but staying below the open expert; additive equality at three bits) and failed by 0.026 in a six-option world that is mostly right — the margin, and the corpse, are printed in Theorem 11′(iii). The floors move with the lower wall of Theorem 9′; where the wall is most of the ceiling, the inversion has nowhere left to stand.

The watcher of Theorem 11 is the strongest possible one — he knows the true structure of Vera’s behavior and updates perfectly. Theorem 20 ran the weak ones, and they are not weaker at the floor: a sequence model told nothing, and a frequency count, both arrive where he does, within days. What had looked like a flattering idealization turned out to be the floor’s name. The only thing that protects a habit from a watcher is the watcher’s wrong theory of it, held firmly.

And one paragraph at the edge of the model, fenced. Where does the coin come from? Inside the mathematics, hh is simply given. Outside it, your coin is your intake of the not-yet-filed: new experience, other minds, imagination — the universe handing you inputs no watcher has seen yet. A hypothesis-agent like Elias (Chapter 8) whose convictions are updated by experiment has a coin exactly as large as his experiments are fresh; a person whose inputs all arrive through channels the watcher also reads has, whatever their inner life, a coin of nearly zero. Whether any inside watcher could in principle capture the whole stream — there being no seats outside the universe — is a question this book flags, fences, and leaves standing. SPECULATIVE Result R6 puts one number under that paragraph: a coin whose source a watcher can learn is a habit one level up, and the file reopens.

Part IV. Towns: Freedom Is Social · Chapter 10

Neighbors

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

No one lives on the harbor alone. The moment a second person appears, something changes that no chapter so far has priced: the neighbor’s actions become part of your circumstances. You watch them — you cannot help it; they are information, standing right there. And this book keeps finding that information is never free to be near.

Two findings, and they cut in opposite directions. First: in a shared world, your capacity for independence is not entirely yours. Every person near you whose behavior visibly tracks the future you share consumes some of your ceiling — because whatever their actions reveal about the common future is something your circumstances now tell any watcher about you. Freedom capacity, in a shared world, is a commons. Second, and against the natural guess: ordinary, imperfect neighbors make your education gate easier to cross, not harder — while one particular kind of neighbor, the flawless and fully visible expert, does not raise your gate but welds it shut entirely.

§2The story: three fields over

Your farm shares one future with the valley — same weather, same river, same market. Consider three possible neighbors on the next field, and what each one’s presence does to you.

Priya farms the ordinary way: she reads the sky and the soil like everyone, right more often than not, wrong in her own fashion. Living beside her costs you something real: her plantings visibly track the valley’s shared future, so anyone watching your circumstances — which now include Priya — learns more about what’s coming for you both, and your ceiling of independence drops by about a fifth. But here is the turn the natural guess gets backwards: Priya makes your gate easier. Because she is imperfect, she and the sky sometimes disagree — and every disagreement is a crack of genuine ambiguity where even a little knowledge of your own becomes the deciding vote. Beside an imperfect neighbor, modest education starts paying almost immediately.

Joss is a Vera of farming — deliberately hard to read, his choices tracking convictions and flips no file contains. He is expensive company for any watcher and cheap company for you: his behavior leaks little about the shared future, so your ceiling barely drops, and his occasional divergences still crack open ambiguity that lowers your gate. The unreadable neighbor consumes almost none of the commons.

Then there is Aldo, whom the valley takes for a sage. Start with the Aldo of his reputation — never wrong, never hidden — because that Aldo’s arithmetic is exact, and it is the ceiling on what any real one can do to you. Beside a flawless visible expert your ceiling of independence is not lowered — it is zero: everything about the valley’s future is readable off his field, so everything you rationally do is readable too. And your gate is not raised — it is welded: no education, at any strength, can make your own knowledge the deciding vote, because there is never a genuine ambiguity for it to decide. Departing from a visible right answer is not independence; it is error. Beside him, everyone becomes the ferry captain.

Now the Aldo who actually farms the next field. He is right about the frost dates, about when the river is too high for the low field, about the price of seed in spring — and so is everyone else; these are the things the valley already knows. Where the year is strange — a late blight, a market nobody has seen — he calls it with the same confidence, and there he is right less often than you are. But a strange year is hard to score: the harvest comes months later, tangled with weather and luck, and nobody keeps the tally by kind of year. The valley keeps one tally for Aldo, and it is a fine one, because most years are ordinary and in ordinary years he is never wrong. So the valley follows him in the strange years too. Chapter 11 runs this valley as a town and counts what it costs: a record earned where the answer was easy is spent where it is hard, and it lasts exactly as long as nobody keeps the second tally.

Sit with the strangeness before the next chapter resolves it. This is not a claim that experts are bad — the next town over will starve for lack of them. It is a conservation statement with an uncomfortable middle: every clearly right, clearly broadcast answer near you makes your own independence both less possible and less necessary — and “less necessary” is doing quiet, dangerous work in that sentence. Whether a valley can live on answers alone, every gate welded and one flawless field wearing the crown, is not a question about two neighbors. It is a question about a fleet, and it has a number, and the number is in Chapter 11.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Theorem 12 The commons, and the welded gate EXACT

Your independence ceiling falls with the legible competence of your neighbors: from 0.77 alone, to 0.71 beside an unreadable neighbor, to 0.61 beside an ordinary one, to exactly 0 beside a flawless visible expert. Your education gate moves the other way: 0.50 alone, 0.18 beside the unreadable, 0.01 beside the ordinary — and beside the flawless expert, no education at any strength opens it. Partial legibility near you opens doors; perfect legibility welds them. (The natural prediction — that legible neighbors raise the gate — runs the other way; the refutation is kept.)

Proposition 15 Diminishing bites EXACT

Each additional ordinary neighbor consumes less of your ceiling than the last: the first costs 0.17, the second 0.13, the third 0.10, the fourth 0.08. Watchable neighbors overlap in what they reveal — so the first one near you matters most, the social twin of “first looks are worth the most” from Chapter 9.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

Your circumstances, enlarged: with a neighbor whose action is visible, the watcher’s seat becomes 𝒪=\mathcal{O} = (your signals, their action), and both your ceiling and your gate are recomputed against that richer seat using the same formulas as Chapters 4–5.

The welded gate, in one paragraph: your rational action follows whichever source wins the reliability race (Chapter 5). Beside Aldo, the enlarged circumstances contain a perfectly reliable entry — his action, which equals the future. A perfect entry cannot lose the race to any education of fidelity less than perfect, in any situation, ever; there are no disagreements left for your knowledge to referee. Hence independence exactly zero and a gate no finite learning opens. Beside Priya, her imperfection guarantees situations where the enlarged circumstances disagree internally — and in exactly those situations, the race is close and your own knowledge can win it at low fidelity. That is why her presence lowers your gate to nearly nothing while still costing you ceiling: the two effects are not opposites but two faces of what her behavior reveals.

Diminishing bites, precisely: neighbors watching the same sky reveal overlapping information about it; the second neighbor can only add what the first did not already reveal. Shared-source information is like light in a room — the second window brightens less than the first.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

Computed by exact enumeration in the shared-future world: one common future, each party with its own signal of it, the neighbor acting first and visibly. The constants travel only with this class. Two audits printed: the gate results were re-derived under a deliberately stricter definition of “the gate opens” and did not move (the jump at the threshold is discontinuous, so definitions cannot disagree); and the natural prediction that legible neighbors would raise the gate was refuted by the computation and is kept in the record — the ambiguity-crack mechanism was found in the wreckage. What this chapter leaves to the next: neighbors who react to you, crowding, and learning across seasons — the towns of Chapter 11 have all three.

§6The code

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing
  • code/neighbors_T12_P15.py — the four neighbor types, the ceiling and gate numbers, and the erosion sequence.
  • code/dichotomy_scaling_and_audits.py — the stricter-gate audit.
  • Formal statements, the kept refutation, and proofs: docs/THEOREMS_v1.md.

Part IV. Towns: Freedom Is Social · Chapter 11

The Fishing Town

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The story
  3. §3The theorems
  4. §4The mathematics
  5. §5The model
  6. §6The code

§1The idea, in plain words

Chapter 10 left a question standing: can a community live on visible right answers alone — every gate welded, one flawless expert wearing the crown? The question needs communities that can fail, and a way to count how often. So this chapter builds a town, feeds it or starves it by exact arithmetic thousands of ways, and reads off what made the difference.

The findings, in advance. What keeps a town alive is not how many decision-makers it has, and not how skilled its best decision-maker is. It is how many genuinely different ways of being wrong it contains. Independence multiplies safety — literally, exponentially. Sameness puts a floor under danger that no amount of skill or size can break. And the strangest line-item on the town’s books: its least competent member, kept fed, is sometimes the only insurance policy that pays.

§2The story: nine boats

Here is the town. Nine fishers. Every morning the fish are somewhere — one of four grounds — and nobody knows which for certain. Each fisher reads the water; each may also have education, years of learning how fish actually move. If most boats find the fish, the town feasts. Three missed days in a row is a famine. The town was run every way it can be arranged. Five lessons came back. (Axiom 2 is what fails in this town, day after day; independence is what contains the failure.)

Lesson one. Nine okay heads beat one excellent head. Give each fisher modest skill: right 70% of days, judging alone. Now hire a harbor master who is right 80% of days, and have everyone follow him. The independent town finds the fish 90 days in 100; the harbor master’s town, 80 — and the independent town’s famine risk is six times lower. When independent fishers err, they err in different directions and the majority still lands on the fish; when the master errs, the whole fleet sails to one empty sea. There is power in the people, and it is not a slogan: every two independent fishers added cuts famine risk roughly in half, doubling and doubling again.

Lesson two. Nine heads with one teacher are one head. Now the nastier town: nine fishers, all educated — by the same tutor. Each still right 70% of days. But when the tutor’s method fails, it fails in all nine heads at once. This town’s famine risk came out exactly equal to a town with a single fisher. Not close. Equal. Nine boats, nine engines, nine lifetimes of skill — one way of being wrong, and therefore one head.

Lesson three. Listen to the master — a little. So should nobody follow the harbor master? Every mixture was tried, and the safest town of all has exactly one boat following him: it imports his higher skill without creating a herd. Each additional follower makes the town less safe, and at five of nine — the moment the followers become a majority — the master decides every day, and nothing added after matters. Centralized wisdom is medicine at a low dose and poison at a herd dose. (The dose is this town’s: a master far better than the room earns a larger one, and a master who misleads earns none — §5.)

Lesson four. Shared blind spots put a floor under your risk. Real tutors overlap; real weather fools whole fleets. Let the fishers’ training share a flaw — some days, everyone’s education points at the same mirage. Lesson one’s exponential protection survives, but only down to a floor: below it, adding fishers does nothing, because the remaining risk is the risk they share. And the floor punishes size. A town of nine barely feels a small shared flaw; a town of thirty-one pays sixteen times over for the same flaw. Big communities are not protected by being big — past modest size, their safety is set almost entirely by what everyone has in common. To make a big town safer, do not add heads. Subtract sameness.

Lesson five. The wildcard. One fisher ignores everything — the master, the tutors, sometimes the birds themselves. He follows hunches. He is right far less often, and on ordinary days he is a small tax on the town’s catch. But on mirage days — when every trained head sails to the same empty sea — the wildcard is somewhere else. In the shared-tutor town, each wildcard cuts the risk of total failure about six-fold. He will never make the town rich: wildcards insure subsistence, not prosperity. The town that keeps a few eats less and starves never. And one warning the arithmetic insists on: in a town whose fishers already err each in their own way, the wildcard helps nothing and costs fish. He is insurance — and insurance is only worth buying against a risk you actually share.

Two more arrangements, run later, and exact. The sage’s tally. Let three days in ten be hard — fog, a strange current — and let one voice in the harbor be right on every plain day and on only half the hard ones, where a single fisher manages 55 in a hundred. Keep one tally per voice and his is the best record in town, 85 against 79, so every boat follows him — and the famine rate doubles. Everything he was right about, the town already knew; every day on which following him made a difference was a hard one. Keep two tallies, plain days and hard days, and he is followed where he is right and nowhere else. And where the fog cannot be seen from the shore, no fisher can be talked out of him: behind the sage each boat is right 85 mornings in a hundred, reading for itself 79, and what is better for each boat is worse for the town. Only where the boats that find the fish must share them does the herd stop itself — at two boats of the nine. The boat that stays in. Let sailing cost something, and let a fisher’s reading be clear some mornings and murky others. A fisher with a murky reading and a costly trip stays ashore, and he is right to. With four boats in ten staying in, the town starves 98 seasons in a hundred where it starved 7: the doubtful boats had been landing four boatloads in ten, and the town was living on them. Nor does his own hunger bring him out. His one boatload turns a bad day into a good one about one morning in four in a town of nine boats, and eight in a hundred in a town of ninety-nine: the larger the town, the less it is any one fisher’s to save.

Lesson six. The town that watched itself. [SIMULATION — this lesson only.] Every number in lessons one through five was exact arithmetic. This lesson’s town learns, which is too tangled for exact enumeration, so its results come from many simulated town-lifetimes with honest bookkeeping inside each: strong evidence, not proof, and boxed so you always know which is which.

The natural prediction, before any of this was built, was that a living town would fix itself: let fishers watch each other’s results, and a master-following fleet converts into the distributed fleet that survives. The living town was built twice, in two worlds that differ by one fact: whether crowding costs anything. The first is the glass sea, named for what it lacks — friction. Nothing a boat does on it leaves a mark on any other boat’s catch: fish are infinite, so every boat on the right ground catches its fill no matter how many boats are already there. There, honest ledgers harden the herd: each fisher correctly learns the master (80%) beats his own reading (70%), and the sharper the fishers reason, the more completely they herd — above ninety percent at the coldest reasoning. Watching results cannot save the glass-sea town, because results teach each fisher that the herd is smart; they cannot teach him that the herd is fragile. The second world is the real sea — real because every ground that has ever been fished works this way: fish are finite, and boats on the same ground split the catch. There the herd dissolves. Not from wisdom; from hunger: nine boats split one ground’s catch nine ways, while the stubborn fisher who trusted her own reading and was right eats alone. Hub-following falls to about half and stays there even among the coldest reasoners — it is the balance point of a real game, not noise — while the town’s accuracy rises and its famine risk is cut in half.

The prediction, scored: as literally stated (results alone convert the fleet), refuted by the glass sea; with one condition added — that fishing a crowded ground costs something — confirmed. The missing mechanism is the one any fisher would name first: wouldn’t they realize they are overfishing one spot, and move? The mechanism in one line: the glass sea is a chorus, where everyone can sing the same note and no note is worth less; the real sea is a potluck, where a dish everyone brings feeds no one. Herding survives wherever joining the crowd costs nothing. And one thought, flagged as interpretation only: ask which of your own economies are glass seas — a fishery punishes crowding automatically; an information feed does not.

Six lessons, one town, two axioms. Nothing about human nature was assumed; nothing about politics. Yet the reader has noticed the town has opinions — about newsrooms and central banks, about school systems teaching one method to a nation, about the strange usefulness of stubborn people. The town is not shy. How far its opinions travel is the next, carefully fenced chapter.

§3The theorems

The machinery, for those who want it

Theorem 13 Survival structure EXACT

(i) Famine probability falls exponentially in the number of independent educated fishers (roughly halving per two added). Nine independent 70%-fishers beat one 80% authority six-fold on famine and outright on daily success. (ii) Fishers sharing one competence source have the famine risk of a single fisher, exactly, at any headcount. (iii) Safety against hub-following is a dose curve whose optimum moves with the expert’s margin: one follower when he is 80–85% against 70% readers, two at 90%, a bloc at 99%; at the printed accuracies, a benefit at one, worsening after, saturating exactly at bloc majority. (iv) Wildcards cut total-failure risk multiplicatively where blind spots are shared, and strictly hurt where they are not.

S1 The living town SIMULATION

Observation alone locks the herd (rational result-watching converges to hub-following); finite resources convert it (interior mix, higher accuracy, famine halved). Lesson six, boxed above; scripts in §6.

S2 The town under stress SIMULATION

Across 972 towns — master accuracy, misdirection, slumps, readers’ bad weeks, shared blindness, a sea with memory — the best dose of following stays below the herd line in 240 of the 243 towns whose readers share no blindness and whose master is right at most nine days in ten, and moves to the bloc where the readers share a blindness or the master is nearly never wrong. The all-readers town is safe only while its errors are independent across readers and across days; that independence is the theorem’s premise and the thing to be protected.

S3 The town that stops reading SIMULATION

Where reading is a skill that fades with disuse and returns with use, the town has one long-run state, reached from a town of readers and from a broadcast town alike: the slacker the crowding and the faster the fading, the nearer that state is to everyone following and no one able to read. No point of no return; a slope with one bottom.

Theorem 14 The correlation floor EXACT

With a shared flaw striking all trained heads together some fraction of days, the exponential of 13(i) survives only down to a floor set by that fraction — and the same small flaw that costs a town of nine a factor of 1.3 costs a town of thirty-one a factor of 16. Correlation taxes scale specifically; past modest size, decorrelation is worth more than growth.

Theorem 21 The public-signal window EXACT

Give every fisher, beside a private reading right with probability pp, one signal all can see, right with probability aa. A fisher who reasons correctly follows the public signal against a disagreeing reading exactly when a>pa > p — and then the whole fleet sails on one signal. Whenever aa lies above each reader’s accuracy and below the accuracy of the readers’ majority, every boat is right more often than before and the town goes hungry more often than before. In the printed town the window runs from 0.70 to 0.901, and famine jumps from 7 seasons in a hundred to 83 at its lower edge. No master, no lie and no shared flaw is assumed: the sameness is manufactured by each fisher’s correct use of what everyone can see.

Theorem 22 The borrowed record EXACT

Let some days be plain and some hard. Let one voice be right on every plain day — when the readers’ majority is right too — and right less often than a single reader on a hard one. A fisher who keeps one tally per voice finds that voice’s record better than his own whenever plain days are common enough, and follows it; the town then fails on its hard days at the voice’s rate where it had failed at its majority’s. In the printed town — three days in ten hard; a reader right nine plain days in ten and 55 hard days in a hundred; the voice right on half the hard days — his record is 85 against a reader’s 79.5, every boat follows him, and famine doubles, from 11 seasons in a hundred to 22.5. On plain days the town’s majority was right 999 times in a thousand: he was credited for telling it what it knew. Two tallies — one for plain days, one for hard — put him back where he is right and the town back at 11. And his standing lasts in exact inverse proportion to the share of hard days whose outcome anyone records against him: a reputation for never being wrong ends at the first recorded miss — a week away when every hard day is scored, seven seasons away when one in a hundred is. Attacked after it was stated (code/attack_T22_T23.py), the theorem came back sharper on one side and bounded on the other. It needs no mistaken fisher: one who knows every number here and cannot tell a hard morning from a plain one is right more often behind the voice than reading — 85 against 79.5 — so following is each boat’s best move and the town’s worst. And it is a theorem of the free answer. Where the boats that find the fish must share them, joining the voice stops paying once two boats are behind him — a third would land 0.109 of the catch where a reader lands 0.111 — and famine stops at 14 seasons in a hundred. The borrowed record rules where agreeing costs the agreer nothing.

Theorem 23 The boat that stays in EXACT

Let a fisher’s reading be clear on some mornings and murky on others, and let sailing cost something. He sails when the reading is worth the trip. Once a trip costs more than a murky reading is worth, the murky boats stay in — each for a sound private reason — and the town loses the boatloads they were landing. In the printed town a 70 percent reader is right nine clear mornings in ten and four murky ones; with four boats in ten ashore on any morning, famine goes from 7 seasons in a hundred to 98. Covering the gap between what a doubtful trip costs and what it is worth brings them back out — for under three percent of the catch when the gap is a twentieth of a boatload. It is Theorem 5b in a boat: a mistake budget is what keeps the doubtful boats on the water. A fisher who counts his own hunger stays in all the same (code/attack_T22_T23.py). Let a bad day cost him a boatload of his own. His trip is then worth his catch plus his chance of saving the day — 27 in a hundred in the printed town — and the murky boats stay in above a trip cost of 0.51 where they had stayed in above 0.40; at three boatloads of hunger, above 0.72. In a town of ninety-nine boats that chance is 8 in a hundred and the line moves from 0.40 to 0.43. His own hunger moves the line and does not remove it, and it moves it less the larger the town.

These theorems have ancestors outside physics, and they should be named. Lesson one is Condorcet’s jury theorem (1785) on independent fishers. Lesson two’s collapse and Theorem 14’s floor are in the spirit of what Ladha (1992), Boland (1989) and Berg (1993) proved for correlated jurors — and what ensemble learning proved again for correlated classifiers (Tumer and Ghosh 1996): a shared flaw sets a floor that no headcount breaks. The wildcard insurance of 13(iv) is ecology’s insurance hypothesis (Yachi and Loreau 1999) — diversity as a buffer against a fluctuating world — and the collapse of a one-tutor town is the loss of what ecologists call response diversity (Elmqvist and colleagues 2003). What this chapter adds is the arrangement: the famine metric as survival over streaks, the shared-tutor identity Neff=1N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1 exactly, and the dose curve of 13(iii) — which the jury literature, studying correlation rather than shared sources, does not contain. Theorem 21’s upper edge is Condorcet’s own number, the accuracy of the majority, and its mechanism stands near two modern results without being either: information cascades (Banerjee 1992; Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch 1992), where agents herd by watching one another’s actions in turn, and the social value of public information (Morris and Shin 2002), where a public signal can lower welfare among agents who want to match one another. In the window nobody watches anybody and nobody wants to match: each fisher would follow the signal alone on the sea. Theorem 22 has an ancestor in the record of expert forecasting: Tetlock (2005) scored some twenty-seven thousand forecasts from 284 experts and found them barely better than guessing, no better than well-read amateurs, and worse than simple extrapolation rules. A doctorate, years of experience and access to classified information made virtually no difference. One thing predicted consistently, and it predicted the wrong way: the better known the forecaster, the further the stated odds sat from what happened. The theorem is in that spirit and adds the mechanism — one tally where two are needed — and the rate at which the standing decays once the second is kept. Theorem 23 is in the spirit of Olson’s logic of collective action (1965) and of the threshold public-goods games of Palfrey and Rosenthal (1984), where each contributor weighs the chance that his own contribution decides the outcome — with this difference: what goes unsupplied here is not effort but doubtful judgment, and the boats that stay in are the careful ones.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it · 3 pictures

Lesson one’s engine is old and honorable: majorities of independent voters. If each of nine fishers is right with probability 0.7, independently, the chance that five or more are right is the sum of the favorable cases — 0.901 — and the chance the majority fails on any given day is 0.099. A famine needs three failures in a row; the book computes that by simple bookkeeping over runs of days (a small table tracking “how long is the current losing streak” — nothing fancier), giving 0.074 per ninety-day season. The all-follow-the- master town fails on exactly the days the master fails — 0.2 — and its famine probability, 0.44, does not improve by one decimal if the town grows, because it contains one way of being wrong.

The shared-tutor identity is bookkeeping of the same kind: nine fishers with one tutor succeed and fail as one body, so every formula reduces to the single-fisher case — headcount cancels out of its own arithmetic. And the correlation floor: if a shared mirage strikes a fraction ρ\rho of days, the town’s daily failure is at least ρ\rho times the mirage’s failure rate no matter how large the majority — a floor that size cannot touch, only sameness can lower.

The window is two lines of the same bookkeeping. A fisher whose reading names one ground while the public signal names another weighs a(1−p)a(1-p) against (1−a)p(1-a)p, and follows the signal exactly when a>pa > p. Once every fisher does, the town fails on the days the signal fails, 1−a1-a, where the reading town failed on the days its majority failed, 0.099. In the printed town the public signal is yesterday’s ground, on a sea that stays put from one day to the next with probability ρ\rho, so a=ρ+(1−ρ)/4a = \rho + (1-\rho)/4. Below ρ=0.6\rho = 0.6 nobody consults yesterday and the town is the reading town. From 0.6 to 0.868 everybody does, and famine runs from 83 percent down to the reading town’s 7.4. Only past 0.868 — a sea steadier than the readers’ majority is accurate — is yesterday the better guide for the town as well as for the boat. The simulated town (code/rig/town_stress2.py) lands on the exact figures: 55 percent at ρ=0.7\rho = 0.7, 3 percent at 0.9. The window belongs to fishers paid for being right whatever the company — the glass sea of lesson six. Where a crowded ground pays less, §5’s arithmetic applies with the public signal in the master’s place: with eight boats on yesterday’s ground at ρ=0.7\rho = 0.7, reading pays 0.218V0.218\,V against following’s 0.086V0.086\,V, and the fleet cannot all sit on yesterday.

§5The model, and what it covers

The machinery, for those who want it

The town is deliberately spare: days independent of each other, fish placed fresh each morning, fishers deciding once per day, all famine probabilities exact. Constants — the six-fold, the sixteen, the “three flips” of the wider book — are properties of this town and travel only with it; the shapes (the exponential, the identity, the dose curve, the floor) held everywhere the town was varied.

The fishers of lessons one through five never learn, never crowd, and never stay ashore. Each of those was then let in. Lesson six lets them learn and crowd. S2 lets their errors persist, their masters mislead and their sea remember. Theorem 21 lets them consult it. Theorem 22 gives them a sage they do not score where it matters. Theorem 23 lets them stay ashore.

Theorem 13 is a theorem about readings, not about who gives the orders. Nine independent readings protect the town whoever dispatches the boats. A harbor master who polls nine fishers and sends the fleet on their majority inherits the same 0.074 in this model; a master who hedges his own single signal gains nothing on the famine metric, because one 80% reading cannot put five boats on two grounds. Independence beats the master only above a right-ground accuracy of about 0.63 (education near one half in this town); below it, independent voting amplifies error, and Chapter 14’s first rule — past the gate — comes before all the others. Whether readings stay independent in a population that never acts on them is answered by the living town, where that arrangement failed — fishers who could see the hub stopped reading for themselves — and the link from acting to reading, once a conjecture, is now a model with a result (S3 above, and Chapter 15): give reading a skill that fades with disuse faster than practice restores it, and a town with any slack in its crowding slides to nine boats in ten behind the hub with its readers at chance, from wherever it starts. And a fleet dispatched from the center is, from the environment’s seat, one free agent and, from the dispatcher’s seat, nine rocks: the most surveilled configuration this book prices (Theorems 9 and 12).

The town’s survival is a majority game — enough boats on the right ground — and Condorcet’s logic is a majority-game logic. Much production is not: a surgery, a flight, a chip succeeds only if every step does (Kremer’s O-ring, 1993), and there independent execution errors multiply into near-certain failure — which is why such work is standardized and scripted, correctly. The book’s independence belongs to the readings in such a task — the independent check, the second pair of eyes, the inspector who does not share the team’s blind spot — not to the hands. Theorem 13 says nothing about conjunctive execution, and the physics theorems of Chapter 2 are not production functions and must not be borrowed as such in either direction.

The payoffs, exactly. The living town de-herds because fishing a crowded ground pays less — but the right inequality is not the naive one. When the reader and the master are both right they share the ground, and the reader’s choice changes the town’s total catch. With eight boats on the master and one deciding: reading pays 0.70(0.80V/9+0.20V)0.70\,(0.80\,V/9 + 0.20\,V) against following’s 0.80V/90.80\,V/9 — 0.202V0.202\,V against 0.089V0.089\,V in the printed town — and because the reader adds to the town’s catch whenever the master is wrong, pooling any share of the catch, up to all of it, leaves reading ahead (0.104V0.104\,V against 0.089V0.089\,V at full pooling). What reverses the ranking is not pooling but the master’s margin: against a 99% master, following pays at every pooling fraction. No winner-take-all is needed, only a crowding penalty and a master who is merely better, not vastly so. Which is also the correction to lesson three: one follower is the optimum when the master is 80–85% against 70% readers; by 90% two followers are safer, by 99% a bloc is — exactly computed, and the dose is set by the expert’s margin and by how his errors correlate, which independent days cannot show — and which was therefore computed, town by town (code/rig/town_stress_T13.py; the clean town reproduces the exact numbers). A master who misdirects on one in ten of the days he knows is still worth one boat, barely; at three in ten he is worth none, at any accuracy up to ninety-nine percent: the margin that sets the dose is the margin net of the lie. A master whose errors come in slumps is worth no boat at eighty percent and one at ninety, and a bloc behind him starves in as many as nineteen seasons of twenty. Readers whose errors persist — bad weeks — lift the all-readers famine from seven percent past fifty. If the master is spared the bad weeks his readers have, the best dose rises to three boats — still under the herd line — and even the bloc beats the town with no followers. Give the master the same persistence and the book’s ordering returns: all readers at fifty-two percent, one follower best, the bloc at ninety-five. And readers who share a blindness on three days in ten are not nine readers: nothing under the herd line survives, and a bloc behind a master whose errors are his own is the best arrangement left — Theorem 14 seen from the other side. A sea that remembers yesterday changed nothing, for fishers who do not consult yesterday; fishers who do are Theorem 21, and inside its window no arrangement of readers helps — only a following behind an honest master more accurate than the sea. A master who fishes for himself, and misdirects once his following is large enough to crowd his own catch, is worth exactly the following that stays under that size: famine is certain above it and unchanged below it, so the insurance a town can buy from him is capped where misdirection begins to pay. The cap binds where it is needed. Readers with bad weeks want three boats or more behind an honest master; a master whose temptation begins at three leaves them two, and famine at 28, 18 and 11 percent where his honest twin leaves 25, 6 and none (code/rig/town_stress2.py). What the stress leaves standing is the structure, not the headline: protection comes from errors that are independent, and the channel worth following is whichever one’s errors are uncorrelated with the rest — sometimes the center’s. “Keep a few wildcards fed” — a transfer to a few — and “fund mistake budgets” — lowering the price of one’s own wrong bet — touch neither the crowding penalty nor the margin.

The same paragraph in numbers: famine, in seasons of a hundred, by how many of the nine boats follow the master (code/rig/results_town/, code/rig/results_town2/; 20,000 simulated seasons a cell; readers right 70 days in a hundred). The self-serving master misdirects once more than two boats follow him.

Part IV. Towns: Freedom Is Social · Chapter 12

A Conjecture, Fenced

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The conjecture
  3. §3What supports it
  4. §4What limits it

§1The idea, in plain words

Fenced: a conjecture, and nothing later depends on it

[SPECULATIVE — everything in this chapter is conjecture. Nothing later in the book depends on it. It is included because it is beautiful and because hiding it would be a different kind of dishonesty.]

Notice what the fishing town never mentioned: humans. Its five lessons were proved about things that know imperfectly, err inevitably, and share a future — any such things, made of anything, anywhere. The theorems do not check your species at the door.

§2The conjecture

Fenced: a conjecture, and nothing later depends on it

So here it is, stated once. Any advanced life, on any world, that satisfies this book’s two axioms — no perfect knowledge, mistakes inevitable — will eventually stumble into distributed error correction, the way chemistry on any world stumbles into the same stable arrangements of matter — the same bonds, the same molecules, found in steps, because matter keeps presenting the same structure to whoever is looking. The survival arithmetic is the same on every substrate for the same reason the arithmetic of bonds is. What humans call democracy would then be one species’ rough, early, still-changing implementation of a universal discovery — the way human laboratories are one rough implementation of the scientific method, which any curious species must also eventually find. Not an invention. An encounter.

§3What supports it

Fenced: a conjecture, and nothing later depends on it

Only this, but it is real: the mathematics of Chapters 4 through 11 truly is substrate-free. The exponential of independent heads, the collapse of shared teachers, the poison of herd-following, the floor of sameness, the insurance of wildcards — none of these mention neurons, ballots, or flesh. A silicon fleet, a fungal network, a civilization of tides would face the same arithmetic. When the same theorem binds every possible student, it is not crazy to expect every long-surviving student to have learned it. The conjecture also has a named ancestor, in whose spirit it is offered: Sen’s observation (1999) that no famine has ever taken place in the history of the world in a functioning democracy — a survival filter noticed in the record before any theorem bound it. Chapter 11’s arithmetic is one candidate for why. The fence stays.

§4What limits it

Fenced: a conjecture, and nothing later depends on it

Nearly everything else. Humanity has met exactly one advanced species, and it is itself — and the ballot boxes, the single feeds, and the welded gates of the present moment suggest that species is still in the early, clumsy chapters of the discovery. A sample of one, still mid- experiment, proves nothing about the curriculum of the universe. There is also a quieter limit, which surfaced while this book was being written: whether any observer inside a universe can ever hold the whole of what feeds another mind’s choices — there being no seats outside — is a question that touches this conjecture’s edges and stays open at its own address (Chapter 15).

§5Why print it at all

Fenced: a conjecture, and nothing later depends on it

Because the alternative is worse. A book that computes for eleven chapters and then pretends to have no view of what the computations suggest is performing modesty, not practicing it. The honest posture is the one this chapter takes: state the beautiful thing once, mark it clearly as unproven, fence it so it cannot pretend to be a result, and leave it where a future reader — or a future species — can test it. Beauty is not evidence. It is, sometimes, a map of where evidence would be worth looking for.

§6Pointers

  • The fence’s terms: the front matter’s label definitions.

Part V

The Ledger

  1. 13The Ledger

Why the self-anointed rule

This part in one paragraph. Where nobody can check an answer, whoever holds standing supplies it. That is how a self-anointed few come to decide the largest parts of other people’s lives — whose time may be taken, what a fair schedule is, what consent is worth — and it is arithmetic before it is anyone’s grievance: Chapter 11 computed it. The remedy is not a better few. It is a ruler in everyone’s hands. The chapters ahead hand it over: the ledger; the strongest defense of the man it audits, and the four answers to it; a national survey, a law and an experiment that already fill its first columns; and what the arithmetic says to do.

Start with where the few do not rule. Nobody — no senator, no billionaire, no committee of laureates — gets to dictate the speed of light. Nobody rules by decree on the energy in a gallon of gasoline. Where an answer can be checked by anyone holding an instrument, authority serves the measurement: the powerful build their bridges and their engines around the numbers like everyone else, and an undergraduate with a good instrument can overrule a king.

Now where they do rule. Whose time may be taken, and at what price. What a fair schedule is. What a worker’s consent is worth. Which communities may be hollowed and called efficient. How much sameness a society can be fed. These govern most of most lives, and they have been governed by whoever had the standing to declare — because nobody could check.

How the standing is acquired is Theorem 22, and it needs no villain. Chapter 11’s town had a sage. On a plain day — seven days in ten — he was always right, and so, 999 days in a thousand, was the town without him: a plain day is one whose answer anyone can check. On a hard day he was right half the time, which is worse than one fisher reading the water for himself. The town kept one tally for each voice, plain days and hard days together, and on that tally the sage held the best record in the harbor: 85 right in a hundred against a fisher’s 79. So every boat followed him, on the hard days as on the plain ones, and the famine rate doubled. His record was earned on the days when following him changed nothing, and spent on the days when it cost the town its fish.

That is the pattern outside the town. A voice earns its record on the questions anyone can check. It is then believed on the questions no one can check, where it is right no more often than anyone else. And its misses there never reach the record, because nobody is keeping score. How long such standing lasts depends on one number: the share of the hard calls that somebody scores. Score every hard day and the sage’s standing is gone in a week. Score one hard day in a hundred and it outlasts seven seasons. Nobody has to be fooled for any of this. A fisher who knows every number in the theorem, and cannot tell on a given morning whether the day is plain or hard, still does better for himself behind the sage — and the town still does worse.

The theorem also says where such a voice will be found. Where a shared answer pays less — a fishing ground, a claim, a crowded trade — the herd stops itself at two boats in nine. Where an answer can be held by everyone at no cost to any holder — a forecast, a doctrine, a verdict on what is fair — nothing stops it. That is the second list above, and it is why the self-anointed are found there and not at the assay office. A fortune works the same way, and faster. The prospector who strikes gold was right once, about gold; the fortune then buys a say in how schools are run, how hours are scheduled, how the rules of the claims office are written — matters on which the strike is no evidence at all — and Chapter 13 gives that purchase its name: premium rights. A gatekeeper works the same way, and slower: the reviewer, the chair, the board that decides which assumptions a field may question holds standing earned on the part of the subject that can be checked, and spends it on the part that cannot. The exhibit below is one such assumption, held for half a century in the hardest science there is.

So the law, stated once: an unmeasured domain is governed by standing, a measured one by measurement, and standing gives way at the rate the measuring spreads. The history of science is the history of domains crossing that line — the heavens, then matter, then life, then mind — and at each crossing those who ruled by declaration did not concede. They did not have to. The instrument passed into too many hands. Historians of measurement have told this story from the other end: Porter’s Trust in Numbers (1995) shows quantification arriving in a domain exactly when its experts can no longer be trusted on their word alone. This part is in that spirit, read forward — it brings the numbers to the domain that has resisted them longest. The mechanism and the rate are Theorem 22, exact; the reach across history is this part’s argument, and the exhibit below is its first case. And a ruler kept by one office is a harbor master holding a ruler: Chapter 11’s arithmetic applies to it unchanged. What carries a domain across is the instrument in many hands — which is why every file this part uses is public, every script is printed, and Proposition 13.1 states what an audited party can and cannot do to the record.

And before anyone answers that societies elect their authorities: the largest study of whose preferences move American policy — Gilens and Page (2014), nearly two thousand policy questions — found the average citizen’s preferences with near-zero independent influence on what was enacted, and organized interests and economic elites with a great deal. The reply of its critics (Bashir 2015; Enns 2015; Branham, Soroka and Wlezien 2017) is that on about nine questions in ten the middle and the affluent wanted the same thing, so the data cannot say whose wish was granted — and that where the two parted, the affluent side carried it 53 times in a hundred. Fifty-three sounds like a coin toss. A coin toss between the household at the center of the income ladder and a household a tenth of the way from its top, on questions where the two want opposite things, is not what one household, one say predicts. And the same reply prints a second count. Over those twenty-two years a policy the affluent wanted and the middle opposed became law 37 times in a hundred; a policy the middle wanted and the affluent opposed, 26. Read that reply in this book’s units. Where the two agree and the affluent would have carried it either way, the average citizen’s agreement decided nothing: the match is a coincidence, and nobody was answerable to anyone. Where they part and the affluent side carries, the outcome is an imposition, bought in the currencies of Chapter 13’s premium rights.

And the agreement itself is weaker evidence than it looks, because a preference can be manufactured by dependence. Nearly three American households in five hold some stock, most of them through retirement accounts, and the holding is wide and thin. Among households that hold any, the typical one in the lower half of incomes holds 12,600 dollars of it and the typical one in the top tenth 608,000; the top tenth of households hold 88 percent of all of it, and the bottom half hold six tenths of one percent (Survey of Consumer Finances, 2022; Federal Reserve, Distributional Financial Accounts, mid-2026). Nor is the holding chosen in the sense the word needs. The employer picks the plan and its menu; since 2025 the law enrolls the workers of a newly created plan unless they object; the fund follows an index; and the keeper of the index decides what enters it. In 2026 one index shortened its waiting rule from three months to fifteen trading days, a newly listed company entered on the fifteenth, and the funds that track the index had to buy some four billion dollars of its stock at whatever the price stood. It fell 15 percent in the next six sessions.

A household whose old age has been tied to the price of shares wants what raises the price of shares, and its wanting it says as much about its choosing as a signature that the rent predicted (Chapter 13, the third answer). Hold the first ruler to the preference: if circumstances predict it, it scored no independence, and “they wanted the same thing” is the ferry captain agreeing with the timetable. Elected is not the same as answerable, and agreeing is not the same as choosing.

The chapters behind you were the crossing. Agency — how much of a person’s action is their own, what builds it, what destroys it, what its destruction costs and who pays — has been given a measure. Gates, floors, frontiers, famine arithmetic: none of it asked anyone’s permission, and none of it consulted anyone’s values. The chapters ahead do the bookkeeping that follows. And the reader should understand exactly what changes at this line, because it is not that the powerful become villains. It is quieter and larger than that: they lose the standing to call it opinion. The manager, the fund, the ministry — each may still argue their arrangement is justified. But they must now argue it against a ledger, in a domain that has crossed the line — where authority is a servant, and an ordinary person with a good instrument can overrule a king.

This part of the book is that instrument, handed over.

The law’s own exhibit

Before the bookkeeping begins, one exhibit — because the law just stated has a sharper corollary that the reader deserves to see demonstrated in the hardest science there is: an unmeasured quantity does not stay neutral. It gets assumed. It happened twice in this book’s own lineage, and the two cases should be kept apart.

The first paper’s case is the fare itself. For half a century the third exit from Bell’s theorem was waved away on an assumption nobody had computed: that as the experiments grew, the share of measurement independence a local account must relax would climb toward all of it — full conspiracy, the door welded shut. Hall priced the smallest case in 2010 and found about a seventh. The general case stayed unpriced for fifteen years, and the dismissal stood on the unmeasured column the whole time. The staircase of Chapter 2 is that column, measured: the fare climbs with every pair of particles and never passes one half. The assumption was not wrong by a little. It was wrong at every size, forever — and it had governed the reputation of an entire exit.

The second paper’s case is a quantity in plain view. The Bell experiments are among the most scrutinized measurements in the history of physics — four decades, escalating rigor, Nobel recognition. Through all of it, one quantity was never bounded below the percent level: the total rate at which detector pairs fire, summed over all outcomes, as the analyzer angles turn. Quantum mechanics says that sum is flat. One solved class of local accounts says it carries a fringe — up to twelve percent deep at full strength, a strength the existing record already rules out; what survives are mixtures in which that class carries at most about a seventh of the detections — a fringe at the percent level or below — and below the percent level the sum has never been bounded. And here is the reason nobody settled it [PROVEN — the hiding theorem, arXiv:2608.18886]: the fringe takes identical values at the two relative angles the canonical experiment compares. Not approximately — harmonic by harmonic, the same number on both sides — so the comparison every textbook test was built around cancels it exactly. The standard experiment is not lazy about this quantity; it is mathematically blind to it. For forty years the sum was checked at the percent level and assumed below it — and everything downstream of the assumption was governed by that assumption rather than by a measurement.

The second paper of this book’s lineage ends by handing over the instrument: a scan protocol, validated in simulation, runnable in hours on standard hardware, that confines every factorizable apparatus artifact to where it cannot imitate the signal, calibrates out the one that does not factorize, and bounds the column either way: flat, and a named family of local accounts is confined an order of magnitude below where the record left it; a fringe surviving the calibrations, and the apparatus has produced a joint dependence on both analyzers that no single pair with fixed imperfections can. (The paper’s newest result says where, on the terrains it tested, the correlation must live if the door is taken: in the pair’s frozen offsets at creation, correlated between the two stations — not in anything either station does alone. That is the one place Bell’s own argument reserves for it.) Whichever way it goes, note what changed the moment the protocol existed: the quantity stopped being a matter of assumption and became a matter of schedule. That is the crossing this book keeps describing, performed in miniature, at the bottom of physics, on the very experiments this book’s license rests on. And note, with equal care, what did not change: the license itself. The door’s price was fixed by counting, in Chapter 2, over every account a local world could keep; the scan decides which of two ledgers the surviving accounts settle in, and a flat result closes no door — it moves the bill.

An ordinary person with a good instrument can overrule a king — or forty years of everyone assuming the king was right.
