§1The idea, in plain words

Everything before this chapter built an instrument. This chapter points it at the world — and then lets the world’s best lawyer answer back.

The claim, plainly: the takings of Chapter 7 are real, measurable, and currently uncounted — and what is uncounted is free, and what is free gets taken without limit. Economics has a word for real costs that one party imposes and nobody books: an externality. Pollution was one, invisible to every ledger on Earth, until it was measured — and the measuring, not the outrage, is what changed what could be argued. This book’s proposal is the same maneuver one rung up: displacement of agency, priced and audited, entered on the books beside every other cost of doing business.

Where would an auditor look? The price list of Chapter 7 says where takings are cheap, so it says where takings will be found: scheduling that fills every gap in a worker’s week; products engineered for churn and distraction; systems that make lives more predictable to their operators; arrangements that hold whole populations just below their education gates. The list knows no company’s name. It predicts only this: wherever extraction optimizes, it will be found parked on these squares. Predictions can be checked.

§2The story: the manager’s defense

Return to the Harbor Grill. Its manager has read Chapter 7 — the chapter that used his schedule as its example of theft — and he has come to defend himself, with the strongest argument his position affords. It deserves to be heard at full strength:

“I priced it in. The instability you call theft is reflected in the wage — and my workers, knowing the schedule’s nature, agreed to work for that wage. A willing seller met a willing buyer. Where is your theft in a signed agreement?”

It is a serious argument. Here are the four answers, in ascending order of force.

First: the defense concedes the ledger. Listen to what “I priced it in” does — it admits the quantity exists. You cannot price a fiction. Five minutes ago the position was that nothing was taken; now the position is that something real was taken and compensated. That is not a rebuttal of this book. That is this book winning its central claim — the quantity is real and belongs on the books — after which the argument is only about the price. Which is exactly where the argument should live.

Second: “priced in” is now an auditable claim — and flat prices cannot match nonlinear harms. The manager paid a wage: one number. But Chapter 7’s arithmetic says the harm is not one number — in its model it is seventy times larger against the time-poor than the time-rich, ten times larger near an education gate, and different between two workers on identical pay. A single rate that never asks where each worker stands can cover everyone only if it is set above the largest harm — and then it overpays everyone else; set anywhere lower, the most-displaced workers are underpaid and the books call it even. Either way the common price is not the harm, and which of the two the manager is doing cannot be read off the wage without the audit. Pricing without measuring is not pricing. It is rounding — in the house’s favor. And the claim is testable: if instability were truly compensated, wages would rise with schedule chaos. Where such labor markets have been examined, the premium has been hard to find: irregular and on-call schedules are most common in the lowest income bracket (Golden 2015), and estimated wage differentials for job attributes of this kind are unstable and often wrong-signed (Mas and Pallais 2017, reviewing them). Workers have priced one piece of the schedule themselves: in Mas and Pallais’s hiring experiment, the average applicant gives up a fifth of the wage to escape a schedule set by the employer on a week’s notice — which the authors attribute largely to aversion to the evenings and weekends such schedules bring, not to unpredictability as such. So the experiment prices the employer’s control of the schedule, not the uncertainty this chapter’s ledger tracks; that price is unmeasured. Whether payroll pays the instability back was then asked of a national survey directly (§2D). At equal schooling and age, the households whose hours the employer varies are paid less, not more — full-time workers included — and in the year the same person’s hours pass into the employer’s hands, household income does not rise. It was not priced in. And where steadier schedules were assigned by lot, the stores that gave them sold more. It was not even paying.

Third — the deep one: the consent he cites was purchased with the very currency he took. An agreement’s validity rests on the agency of the person agreeing — the capacity to weigh alternatives, model futures, negotiate. Those capacities are exactly what time poverty and gate-proximity degrade; that is not sentiment, it is the price list. So a feedback loop hides inside the defense: past displacement lowers the price at which future displacement gets “accepted.” And the book can measure this with its own instrument — apply the two rulers to the act of signing itself. If a watcher who knows only a worker’s circumstances — rent due, no savings, every other kitchen in town running the same schedule — can predict the signature with near certainty, then the signing scored an independence of nearly zero. That alone decides nothing — Chapter 4 built the book on the fact that one ruler cannot: a predictable yes to a generous offer is the ferry captain, competent and unreadable to no one. The second reading is not the signing’s aim — a yes that everyone gives carries no information about anything — but Chapter 7’s quantity: the contract’s net displacement of the worker’s frontier, against the named baseline of the worker without it. A predictable yes to an arrangement that expands the frontier is the captain sailing the timetable; a predictable yes to one that contracts it is a person with no port left to choose. The two readings together say how much choosing was in the choice. The law’s “voluntary” is a yes-or-no box; measured independence is a dial; and the defense requires confusing the two. The book need not claim the workers were coerced. It invites the manager to publish both numbers.

Fourth: even a perfect private price cannot settle the public account. Suppose the manager truly, individually, correctly compensated every worker. The town’s ledger still shows a loss, because Chapter 11 priced what degraded, dependent decision-makers cost everyone else: fewer independent heads, weaker error correction, children raised below their parents’ time floors — displacement landing on people who never signed his agreement. A factory paying its own workers a smoke premium has not settled the neighborhood’s account. Private wages cannot buy back a public exponential. (Chapter 14 §5C runs it in the economists’ own model: scored one household at a time, cash is the better remedy; scored by whether the town survives, it does nothing.) That is the textbook meaning of an externality — Pigou’s divergence of private from social cost (1920), and the gap that Coase (1960) himself said bargaining closes only when bargaining is free, which here it is not — and the reason this chapter’s title is not “the wage” but “the ledger.”

The manager’s defense, answered in full: it proves the quantity exists, asserts a price it never computed, rests on consent its own practice degrades, and settles with the only parties who signed — who were never the only parties owed. And notice what the book never called him: evil. It called him unaudited — the one charge a signature cannot answer.

It is also a charge only an audit can settle, and a small one has been run. It begins with something one of his workers would tell the auditor, because she knows what a spreadsheet does not. Nadia: “Don’t ask whether my hours change. Ask who changes them. When I swap a Thursday with Tomas, the week is still mine. When he moves it, the week is his.” Two schedules can look the same on paper and be opposite things to the person living them. The difference is whose hand is on the eraser.

A national survey asks her question. Each autumn the Federal Reserve asks some eleven thousand adults how they are managing, and asks the employees among them whether their hours are normally the same, vary at their own request, or vary on the employer’s needs. Employees whose hours vary at their own request are, on getting by and on savings, not distinguishable from employees on fixed hours. Employees whose hours the employer varies are more often just getting by and more often behind on bills, and their households are paid less, not more. Among them, the ones told three weeks ahead look like fixed-hours employees; the ones told later do not. And when the same person is followed from one year to the next, the strain is there in the year the employer holds the schedule and not in the year he does not. A survey shows a pattern, not a cause — so two tests that can show a cause were run, by others. Seattle required its large retail and food chains to post schedules two weeks ahead and to pay for late changes; set beside workers at the same chains in twenty-four other cities, Seattle’s had fewer short-notice schedules, less hardship and better sleep. And one national retailer assigned twenty-eight stores by lot, nineteen to steadier schedules and nine to business as usual. The steadier stores sold 7 percent more.

What the files show is what she said: the harm follows the hand on the eraser, not the variation. The counts, the tests that were written down before the files were opened, and what none of the three measures — a time floor, a gate, aim — are in §2D.

§2BThe ledger of imposition

The machinery, for those who want it · one picture

One structural result belongs here, because it explains where the takings pool. Model a hierarchy of bounded agents — an executive over regionals over managers over workers — with uncertainty arriving at the top (a demand that varies by some fraction of itself) and each level able to absorb only what its resources allow, passing the remainder down, where it lands whole on every person below. Hours partition: if two of twenty shifts are cut, two people lose the hours. Uncertainty does not: all twenty face will it be me, and when the shortfall is a fraction of demand each worker’s share of doubt is the same whatever the headcount. The cascade is a theorem about the second quantity, and that is the one this chapter prices. Computed exactly EXACT within model: the executive’s resources let him cushion sixty percent of the uncertainty that reaches him, so only forty percent of it goes downhill; a worker can cushion seven percent of what reaches him, and the other ninety-three lands on his life as it is. The worker faces less absolute variance than the executive did — the cascade thins it on the way down — and still loses ten times more agency per person, because the least capacity meets the highest price per unit (the elasticities of Chapter 7). In the reference cascade, the bottom layer bears 93.4% of all agency destroyed — a share: how the gross loss distributes across the layers, measured against a world with no shortfall. What part of it is a taking is a different number, measured against the firm’s cheapest feasible arrangement of the same shortfall, and is stated below. Imposition narrows going up and multiplies going down — not because anyone at the top is a villain, but because passing variance downhill is every bounded agent’s path of least resistance. The cascade needs no conspiracy. It needs only gravity. Two fairnesses the ledger owes the firm, both printed. The firm is a filter: a worker inside the hierarchy faces forty percent of the customers’ raw unpredictability; a solo artisan would face all of it — which is Coase’s reason firms exist, and the ledger’s claim is only that what the firm chooses to pass down is unpriced. And the broadcast is a scheduling rule, not a law of nature: it is the un-tiered on-call pool, where every worker is a candidate for every cut. Whether concentrating the same shortfall on a small on-call tier does less damage depends on where the pool sits: above the gate the time curve is concave and spreading a small cut costs less (Jensen’s inequality, the same seventy-fold of Chapter 7 working in reverse); near the gate, where a spread cut would drag the whole pool toward the cliff, concentrating it on a tier compensated to stay above its own gate costs less. Rule three of Chapter 14 is stated with that boundary. And the two numbers of this section must be kept apart: the 93.4% is a gross share, against no shortfall; the taking is what the actual arrangement destroys beyond the firm’s cheapest feasible arrangement of the same shortfall — which, for a pool well above its gate, can be nothing at all, and for a pool near it, is the whole difference between the un-tiered pool and the paid tier. Management cybernetics drew this picture decades ago: Beer’s viable system (1972; the variety engineering made explicit in 1979) has each level attenuate the variety it can and pass the rest, and Simon’s architecture of complexity (1962) explains why hierarchies are built that way. Supply-chain theory knows the same algebra running the other direction — the bullwhip effect (Forrester 1961; Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang 1997), where demand variance amplifies upstream through orders. The ledger of imposition is in the spirit of both and differs from each in one word: it tracks uncertainty broadcast downward through authority, multiplied by headcount, and prices what it destroys.

The cascade, written out (code/imposition_cascade_T17.py). Uncertainty VV arrives at the top. A person at level ll faces vlv_l, absorbs what a capacity clc_l allows, and passes the remainder whole to every person below; the agency lost is what is faced, times that level’s elasticity εl\varepsilon_l (Chapter 7):

v1=V,vl+1=vl−min(vl,cl),loss per person=εlvlv_1 = V, \qquad v_{l+1} = v_l - \min(v_l, c_l), \qquad \text{loss per person} = \varepsilon_l\, v_l

The reference cascade, each person at one level directing four at the next:

Level People Uncertainty faced, each Absorbed, each Elasticity Agency lost, each Agency lost, level
Executive 1 100 60 0.008 0.80 0.8
Regional 4 40 20 0.02 0.80 3.2
Manager 16 20 6 0.1 2.00 32.0
Worker 64 14 1 0.565 7.91 506.2

The worker’s row is 93.4 percent of the last column, and 7.91 against 0.80 is the ten of the text. The capacities and elasticities are the model’s constants; the two elasticities at the ends are Chapter 7’s, time-rich and time-poor.

Two corollaries, tagged. First ARGUMENT, anchored: formally universal rights bundle a nominal tier and a responsiveness tier priced in exactly the currencies this ledger tracks — time past the gate, mistake budget, protected privacy — so rights-effectiveness inherits the ledger’s distribution. The largest empirical study of American policy responsiveness is evidence consistent with the responsiveness tier being priced. Call them premium rights; their most concrete instance is the purchased mistake budget — too big to fail is the right to err, sold in tiers, socialized at the bottom. Second CONCEPT, modelable: theft compounds. The frontier is defined at the system’s current capacity, and agents operating at their frontiers are what expand it — so stolen agency doesn’t just harm its victim today; it forecloses the expansions the victim would have contributed to everyone’s tomorrow. A stolen hour is a stolen future at interest.

[INTERPRETATION — a resonance, not a premise. The book’s theorems stand without this box.]

The same bookkeeping, at the bottom of physics. Chapter 7 showed that stochasticity is transferred, not destroyed: suppress the visible signature of an imposition in one channel and the bill surfaces in another, at an exchange rate you can compute. It is worth knowing that this accounting pattern is not a metaphor this book invented. In the physics this book’s lineage rests on, the same structure appears as a theorem-grade trade-off: within the solved family of local accounts of the two-particle experiment, any account that hides its detection signature — a specific modulation in the total coincidence rate — below two percent must thereby pay at least 45% of the full measurement-dependence price in that column; below one percent, 68%; below half a percent, 80% [EXACT along the stated family, and a statement about that family only: flat-rate accounts exist outside it at lower detector efficiencies, so flatness alone forces no payment — arXiv:2608.18886, §8–9]. Within the family, the bill never vanishes. It moves between ledgers at a posted rate, and every ledger it moves to has its own observable signature. When this part of the book argues that destroyed agency, priced at zero, does not thereby cease to exist but lands somewhere on someone — the reader should know that the deepest physical theory in existence runs its books the same way. That is a resonance, and this book claims it as nothing more. But it is a well-earned one.

§2CWhat the market’s eyes cannot see

The machinery, for those who want it

The manager’s defense rests, in the end, on a kind of evidence: the record of what people chose, at what prices, under what circumstances. Revealed preference. It is the evidence economics trusts most, and it is worth asking, in this book’s own units, what it can see.

The record is the joint pattern of action and circumstance — which option was taken, and what the observable situation was. Call it choice data. Chapter 4’s first ruler is a function of choice data alone: independence, δA\delta_A, is identified by it exactly. The second ruler is not.

Theorem 19 The hiding theorem, economic [PROVEN by construction; interval endpoints NUMERICAL]

(i) Independence is identified by choice data. (ii) Aim is not: for any fixed choice data, aim ranges over an interval whose lower end reads the residual unpredictability as noise and whose upper end reads it as hidden competence. (iii) The interval is wide. Two exact pairs: uniform choice data — every option equally likely in every circumstance — is produced by pure scatter at aim zero and by Ines’s plateau strategy at aim c0c_0, identically; and choice data of the form “follow the room half the time, scatter otherwise” is produced by a town of Tomases and Nadias at aim 0.07 — and, identically, by the sage, acting on perfect knowledge of the future through a half-reliable world, at aim 1.00. (iv) The standard welfare measure of random-utility economics assigns every point of the interval the same number: the destruction of aim is not mis-estimated by that model; it is invisible to it. (v) Recording the realized future beside the action — the state of the world the action was a bet on, realized afterward and lying outside the audited party’s control, linked to what the person chose — collapses the interval to a point.

Read (iii) again, slowly, because it is the chapter’s thesis in one line. The perfectly competent agent and the near-aimless town leave the same fingerprint in every dataset economics calls revealed preference. A market that scores only choices and prices cannot tell the Harbor Grill’s Nadia from a sage who happens to disagree with the room, and it cannot tell the Grill’s Tomas from a sage in a world the room usually gets right. Whatever was done to them is, in that record, indistinguishable from taste.

The column that sees it is the one the standard record omits: outcomes linked to choices — the same person’s actions and what their future actually held. Panels that follow people over years are, in this book’s terms, the economic torus scan; cross-sections of choices and prices are the four canonical angles. [The congruence, as a resonance and nothing more: a quantity the canonical data cannot see — not approximately but exactly, harmonic by harmonic, because the comparison that data makes takes the same value on both sides — together with the instrument that sees it. Chapter 2’s sequel found the same shape at the bottom of physics. The theorem here stands on its own arithmetic.]

§2DA column from public data

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing · 2 pictures

[DATA — descriptive, not causal; each test below was written down before the files it was run on were opened, or before it was computed.] One column of §4’s audit can be filled from a public file. Each autumn the Federal Reserve’s Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking asks some eleven thousand adults how they are managing, and in each of its 2019 to 2023 files it asks employees whether their hours are normally the same, vary at their own request, or vary on the employer’s needs: the same variability with a different hand on the eraser — the distinction this chapter’s ledger turns on, and one a wage statistic cannot see.

In the 2022 and 2023 files (11,503 employees), hours that vary on the employer’s needs become rarer at every step up in household income, from 28 percent of employees in the lowest band to 11 in the highest. At equal household income band, education, age, gender, race and ethnicity, marital status and children, the employees whose hours the employer varies are more often just getting by or worse (7 points), more often without three months of savings (5), more often unable to meet a four-hundred-dollar expense (3), and more often behind on bills because income varied (11) than employees on fixed hours. Employees whose hours vary at their own request are not distinguishable from fixed-hours employees on the first three. And among those whose hours the employer varies, the ones told three weeks ahead look like fixed-hours employees; the ones told later do not.

That much was looked at freely, and a free look proves little. So three statements were written down — the gap belongs to the employer’s control and not to variability; it is absent at three weeks’ notice; the lowest incomes carry it most — and run unchanged on the 2019, 2020 and 2021 files, which had not been opened (18,268 employees). All three held. Employer-varied against self-varied hours: 7.5 points on just getting by, 5.5 on bills, 2.4 on the four-hundred-dollar expense, each distinguishable from zero, and 1.5 on the three-month fund, which is not. Less than three weeks’ notice against three weeks or more: 10.5 points on just getting by and 8.9 on bills, with the long-notice group 2.4 points below fixed-hours employees on the first, a difference not distinguishable from none. The share on employer-varied hours fell at every step of household income, from 28 percent to 12.

Two further tests were written down before they were computed. The survey re-interviews part of its panel, so one person can be followed from one year to the next: 4,816 employees, 7,390 pairs of adjacent years. In the year a person’s hours are in the employer’s hands, that person is 3.0 points more likely to be just getting by and 6.1 points more likely to be behind on bills because income varied than in the year they are not; hours passing to the worker’s own request bring no change distinguishable from none on either; and the difference between the two changes is itself distinguishable from zero on both measures (5.6 and 3.8 points). Nothing fixed about a person — schooling, temperament, the kind of work chosen — can produce that. And holding industry fixed, across twenty-four industry groups and all five years, removes less than a tenth of the gap: these are not simply restaurant and retail jobs.

The first reply an economist makes to all of this is that it is what a priced-in schedule would look like: if unstable hours were paid more, then at equal income the worker on unstable hours would be the worse off by construction. The reply has a consequence that can be checked, and the check was written down before it was computed: the pay should be higher. It is lower. At equal schooling, age, gender, race and ethnicity, marital status and children, households whose hours the employer varies sit a fifth of an income band below households on fixed hours, and are 5 points less likely to reach fifty thousand dollars a year; among full-time workers alone the gap is 0.15 of a band. And in the year the same person’s hours pass into the employer’s hands, household income does not rise: no change distinguishable from none, and the largest raise the files leave room for is three hundredths of one band.

What the survey carries, and what it does not. Savings did not move within the person: the four-hundred-dollar and three-month measures show nothing in the year-to-year test, where strain and bills do. Entering an employer-varied schedule is distinguishable from staying out of one; leaving has the committed sign and is not distinguishable from staying in. The strain estimate, though not the bills estimate, loses its distance from zero when the survey’s weights are dropped. One thing the free look suggested did not survive: that income varies as much under long notice as under short — in the unopened files it varies less. The 2021 file alone shows the three-week break weakly, and two of the three unopened years were pandemic years. The year-to-year estimates are about half the size of the cross-sectional ones, which is what either selection into jobs or misreported schedule types would produce, and the survey cannot say which: of those whose hours the employer varied in one year, half report otherwise the next. A change of schedule usually arrives with a change of job, and a household already in trouble may take the job on offer; following a person removes what is fixed about them, not what happens to them. Household income is a band, not a wage. And nothing here measures a time floor, a gate, or aim.

What the survey says: a quantity the manager’s defense treats as priced moves with who holds the schedule, in the direction the ledger gives, in data collected for another purpose. (code/field/ and its results/; docs/SHED_PREREG_v0.1.md, v0.2, v0.3. The survey’s files are public and are not redistributed with this book.)

Two designs that can attribute have been run, by others, and they point the same way. When Seattle required its large retail and food chains to post schedules two weeks ahead and to pay for late changes, workers there were compared, before and after, with workers at the same chains in twenty-four other metropolitan areas (Harknett, Schneider and Irwin 2021). Relative to those cities, short-notice schedules fell 11 points and unpaid last-minute changes 13 — and material hardship fell 10 points and sound sleep rose 11. And when twenty-eight stores of one national retailer were assigned by lot — nineteen to steadier schedules, nine to business as usual — the steadier stores’ sales rose 7 percent over the thirty-five weeks of the trial, and each hour of their labor brought in 5 percent more (Williams, Lambert, Kesavan and colleagues 2018). That second result answers a question the first two leave open: what steadiness costs to provide. The experimenters put the added revenue at 2.9 million dollars and the out-of-pocket cost at about 31,000. In that experiment it paid for itself. And in a survey of 27,792 hourly workers at eighty of the country’s large retail and food-service companies, the schedule predicts distress, poor sleep and unhappiness much more strongly than the wage does (Schneider and Harknett 2019). The instability was not priced in, and it was not paying.

§3The claims, tagged

The machinery, for those who want it

The displacement claim. EXACT, model class Theft has a size (Chapter 7’s definition), sizes add, and the price list ranks where taking is cheap — with no assumptions about any taker’s costs.

The schedule-control column. DATA — descriptive In a public survey, financial strain moves with who holds the schedule and not with whether hours vary; it is absent at three weeks’ notice; it follows the same person from year to year; and the households on such schedules are paid less, not more (§2D). Association, tested out of sample and within person; not attribution.

The parking prediction. CONJECTURE, testable Extraction that optimizes — by design or by blind trial — will be found concentrated on the high-yield squares: time of the time-poor, knowledge near gates, legibility of the covert, sameness at scale. No conspiracy is required or alleged: ordinary profit-seeking discovers cracks the way water does.

The audit program. BEGUN Mapping the model’s quantities onto measurable life — schedule entropy, planning horizons, feed sameness, gate proximity — and testing the parking prediction against data. Three columns are filled in §2D, by a survey, a law and an experiment; §4 specifies the rest, and Chapter 15 says what each remaining column requires.

§4The mathematics

The machinery, for those who want it

The auditable object: for a person or population, the displacement Δ\Delta = (where their frontier position was, or would have been) minus (where the practice under audit left it), on both rulers of Chapter 4. The price list converts practices into predicted Δ\Delta per unit of resource taken; the audit runs the arrow backward, from observed lives to implied takings. Three quantities a field audit would estimate, all with model definitions: a person’s time floor (hours past the time gate), their gate distance (education relative to their world’s predictability), and their schedule entropy (how little of their coming hours is settled in advance), and their mistake budget (the error one bad month can survive, Theorem 5b) — each an estimator of position on the (aim, δA\delta_A) plane of Chapter 4. The manager’s defense, in these terms, is the claim that his wage equals Δ\Delta times a fair price — a claim with two free numbers in it that his ledger has never contained.

Proposition 13.1 The ledger cannot be gamed into a better position PROVEN

Let a ledger score a population on both rulers with the future recorded. Let any party post-process the population’s actions using anything it sees — the actions, the circumstances, private noise — but not the future. Then: (i) aim cannot be raised above what the people and the room already jointly know; (ii) independence cannot be raised at a better exchange rate than the frontier’s; (iii) raising independence by injected noise lands visibly inside the frontier; and (iv) the information an action carries about the future beyond what the circumstances already say — I(A;F∣E)I(A;F \mid E), the lower wall of Theorem 9′ — cannot be raised at all. A population already on its frontier cannot be moved past it. A population inside the frontier can be moved toward it by a processor who sees the circumstances, by this construction: rewrite each action as a function of the action, the circumstances and a private coin, and the recorded aim rises from 0 to 0.46 while independence rises too, because the circumstances knew the future and the rewrite laundered that knowledge into the action column. What that rewrite cannot do is raise the conditional information, which fell from 0.81 to 0.35 in the same construction. So the conditional information is the un-inflatable part of the record — the one number the audited party cannot make larger — and an audit records it beside the two rulers as a check, not in their place: on its own it scores the captain and the sage at their independence and nothing more, and it cannot tell a Tomas from a Nadia, which the two rulers can. (The population in the construction, with no unconditional aim and full conditional information, is one whose actions encode the future only in combination with the room — a private channel disguised as noise; a population with no private channel scores zero on it, which is why it is a check and not a ruler.) Two more safeguards the audit needs. The action alphabet is quotiented by consequence: two labels with identical effects on every future are one action, or an operator can inflate independence for free by appending randomized choices that decide nothing (one irrelevant bit lifts a sage’s reading from 0.81 to 0.91 with aim unchanged). And life-plane futures that leave an outcome on a record are rare per person — a night class, a treatment, a venture, a handful in a decade; most of what a life is spent on leaves none — so their information is estimated on cohorts facing shared exogenous shocks, never on one worker’s few decisions, where the finite-sample bias alone exceeds the dial. (Clause (i) is the data-processing inequality; (ii) the definition of the frontier; (iii) Chapter 6’s first kept corpse; (iv) data processing conditional on EE.)

The attack surface that remains, printed at full strength: the immunity is against manipulating actions, not definitions. If the audited party is allowed to define the future against which aim is scored — its own targets, its own measures of success — or to define which circumstances count as the room, then aim is measured against a chosen mark and the proposition does not apply. The defense is procedural, not mathematical, and it is the audit’s first rule: the future must be an outcome the audited party does not choose, recorded by someone it does not pay. Its second rule: the future must be one the audited party cannot manufacture from the action. The gaming it names: a piece-rate escalator on which a worker’s recorded outcome is a function of compliance scores aim at 1.00 for a trapped worker, because control reads as foresight. The column that defeats it is the one Chapter 4 defined — an exogenous future: what the economy came to want, what the illness was, where demand sat — which a night class, a treatment or a side business succeeded by matching, and which no employer’s payout schedule can write.

The audit, specified. What the chapters above require of any field audit, collected in one place so that a reviewer can check the design against it rather than reconstruct it.

Quantities. Two rulers per person or population — independence H(A∣E)/log|A|H(A \mid E)/\log |A| and aim I(A;F)/H(F)I(A;F)/H(F) (Chapter 4) — with the conditional information I(A;F∣E)I(A;F \mid E) recorded beside them as the un-inflatable check (Proposition 13.1). Three estimators of position on the plane: time floor, gate distance, schedule entropy; a fourth, the mistake budget, where it can be had.

The future column. (1) An outcome the audited party does not choose, recorded by someone it does not pay. (2) An outcome the audited party cannot manufacture from the action — the economy’s demand, the illness, the market, never a payout schedule. (3) Life-plane futures estimated on cohorts facing shared exogenous shocks, never on one person’s handful of decisions.

The action column. (4) The alphabet quotiented by consequence: two labels with identical effects on every future are one action. (5) Hand-to-mouth status, where it is an outcome, measured as a band — liquid savings within a fortnight’s income of the limit, as the field already measures it — never as the limit itself (Chapter 14 §5C).

The ledger’s baseline. (6) Every entry against a named feasible alternative (Chapter 7 §1); for a firm’s shortfall, its cheapest feasible arrangement of the same shortfall, not a world without it. (7) Identifying a loss is not attributing it; a design that can tell cause from company is required before a practice is charged. (8) The line between taking and winning is borrowed from property and law, not drawn by the instrument.

What a design can resolve. (9) Any comparison of instruments — time against money, stability against wages — must hold prices or model them; the ranking reversed between the two in Chapter 14 §5C. (10) One cross-section at survey scale can establish that the time tax arrives as a threshold; it cannot certify the threshold’s sharpness finer than about a quarter of the free-time range (Chapter 15 §4). (11) Estimates are regime-specific: a response measured under one schedule regime does not carry to another. (12) Hand-to-mouth status is the least stable signature of the mechanism across the model’s constants; the price of credit and the stock of wealth are the stable ones (Chapter 14 §5C), so a design that scores only hand-to-mouth status can miss a mechanism that is present.

§5What is established, and the applicability program

The machinery, for those who want it

The constants are the model’s; the shapes are what travel. What the small worlds establish is what pollution science had at its beginning: the quantity exists, the instrument works, and the direction of every effect is proven. What the world has added so far is in §2D: a national survey in which strain follows who holds the schedule, a law whose passage lowered hardship, and an experiment in which steadier schedules sold more. The section that grows from here — real cases run through the instrument, of which the manager is the first — is the Applicability program, and its cases must each be done with the same care this one received: the defense at full strength first.

The rulers are substrate-free; nothing in them distinguishes a person from a firm. A company with a private model of the future and actions the regulator cannot predict from public data has independence and aim relative to the regulator’s seat, and an audit that extracts its model — as any action–outcome log does, by Theorem 11 — displaces it. The ledger records that displacement like any other; an instrument that read only one way would be a weapon. What keeps the books from cancelling to zero is not a moral clause but arithmetic the ledger already carries: the same unit of displacement destroys more agency the lower it lands (Theorem 10), and it is multiplied by headcount (the cascade). A regulator’s displacement of one firm and a firm’s displacement of a thousand workers are both entries; they are not the same size — and a firm’s entry is not weighted one either: its workers ride in its boat, so a displacement of the firm’s model is weighted by everyone downstream of it, and an audit that homogenizes an industry’s models is the regulator committing the sameness of Chapter 11 at the scale of the economy. The audit this book proposes records outcomes beside actions; it prescribes no method, for that reason. Two more things the rulers never score, said plainly. They do not score an agent’s targets: an embezzler disguising routine around a private aim stands on the same coordinate as Ines. The ledger catches him elsewhere — on other agents’ planes, where his takings land as displacements (Chapter 7) — not by reading his; and it catches him only as a magnitude. A displacement on a counterparty’s plane looks the same whether it was won by a better product or taken by a bribe, and a theft diffused to a dollar apiece across millions of buffered people registers almost nothing on any of their planes. The ledger measures how much was displaced, against a named entitlement; what counted as taking rather than winning was settled before the ledger opened, by property and by law, and the book borrows that line rather than drawing it. And who counts at all is set by the survival metric chosen, which Chapter 11 states.

Part V. The Ledger · Chapter 14

What the Model Says to Do

  1. §1The idea
  2. §2The seven rules, each with its receipt
  3. §3The observation, stated once
  4. §4Where the list and the monuments disagree
  5. §5What kind of claim this is
  6. §5BThe ledger runs both ways
  7. §5CInside the economists’ own model
  8. §6The receipts

§1The idea, in plain words

This book promised no opinions, and it will not start now. What follows is not advice, and it is not a program. It is a list of what, inside the mathematics, made agents capable and towns durable — ranked by the same arithmetic that priced the thefts, with no moral premise anywhere in the machinery. The reader may do with the list what they wish. The chapter’s real business comes after the list: an observation about it, stated once, exactly, and not inflated.

§2The seven rules, each with its receipt

Get people past their gates. Education below the threshold buys zero independence; just past it, the highest leverage in the entire price list. A society that stops teaching at “almost enough” has paid most of the cost of education and bought none of this particular good. (Chapter 5.)

Put floors under time, and start at the bottom. An hour returned to the time-poor yields on the order of a hundred times the agency of an hour returned to the time-rich (seventy-fold in proportional terms, nearer two-hundred-fold per hour), because the most valuable hours anyone owns are the first few past the time gate — which are exactly the hours the time-poor lose first. If a society can protect only one thing, the arithmetic is not ambiguous about which. (Chapter 7.)

Match the shortfall to where the pool sits. When demand falls short, hours partition but uncertainty broadcasts: an on-call pool of everyone makes every worker face will it be me. Above the time gate, spread the cut — the curve is concave there and a small shared loss costs least. Near the gate, where a shared cut drags everyone toward the cliff, concentrate it on a small on-call tier paid enough to stay above its own gate. The un-tiered pool of workers already near their gates — the arrangement the schedule data describe — is the worst of the four. (Chapters 7 and 13.)

Treat privacy as infrastructure, not amenity. A few honest flips per decision, given jurisdiction over the big choices, make the deepest file worthless — provided the flips are flips: a coin whose generator a watcher can learn is a habit one level up, and the file reopens. Wired narrow, no amount of wildness helps. The difference between those two arrangements is the difference between a person and a file. (Chapters 8–9.)

Subtract sameness. Past modest size, a community’s safety is set by what its members share — one curriculum, one feed, one method — not by its headcount. Nine heads with one teacher are one head. To make a big town safer, diversify the teachers and break up the mirrors. (Chapter 11.)

Dose central wisdom by its margin. Experts are medicine; blocs are poison — when the expert is only somewhat better than the room. The printed town was safest listening to its best-informed voice with exactly one boat; a far better expert earns a larger dose, and the rule is to set the dose by the margin — net of any misdirection — and by how the expert’s errors correlate, never by the expert’s say-so, and never by a record that mixes plain days with hard ones (Theorem 22): the channel worth following is the one whose errors are independent of the room’s. (Chapter 11.)

Keep a few wildcards fed. They cost fish on ordinary days and are the only boats on the water when every trained head sails to the same mirage. They insure subsistence, never prosperity — and only in towns that share blind spots, which is to say, in every real town. (Chapter 11.)

§3The observation, stated once

Stand back from the list. Education for all. Rest for the overworked, the poorest first. Privacy. Pluralism. Distrust of concentrated authority. Shelter for the stubborn and strange.

The reader has seen this list before — on monuments, in scriptures, in declarations written by people who never heard of a conditional entropy. This book put no morality into the machine, and the machine handed back a recognizable portrait of it anyway — as if what the traditions call decency were survival arithmetic, learned the long way, by trial and by grief. The reader holds the evidence and may judge it.

The observation is stated, and stops there. Perhaps morality is the species’ compressed memory of theorems it could not yet write down. Perhaps the resemblance is partial coincidence. The one thing the resemblance is not, any longer, is unarguable either way. It has numbers now.

§4Where the list and the monuments disagree

A resemblance claimed by advocates should be audited like any other claim, so here is the place the list and the monuments disagree — printed, not hidden. Tradition praises the stubborn universally; the arithmetic does not. The wildcard rule is conditional: where error sources are already independent, wildcards help nothing and cost fish. The model’s shelter for the strange is insurance against shared blindness, not reverence for strangeness itself — a colder and more precise kindness than the monuments carve. Readers who find more mismatches are doing exactly what the book asks; Chapter 15 is where such findings belong.

§5What kind of claim this is

It does not say these rules are good. “Good” is a word the machinery cannot produce; the machinery produces “survived” and “was capable,” and the bridge from is to ought remains the reader’s to walk, as it has always been. What the chapter removes is something narrower and arguably more valuable: the claim that such rules are mere preference — soft sentiment against hard realism. Whatever else the seven rules are, they are also engineering. The realist who dismisses them now argues with arithmetic, not with tenderness.

§5BThe ledger runs both ways

One direction, stated as arithmetic and nothing more. Everything in this book that prices theft also prices gift: the same exponential that made famine risk halve with every two independent fishers is, read forward, the return curve on investing in other people’s independence. Helping a neighbor past their gate, funding a stranger’s mistake budget, defending someone else’s privacy — in the town model these are not charity; they are purchased survival for the helper, because every genuinely independent head added protects everyone, multiplicatively. An economy oriented around moving people to their frontiers — and then past them, since reached frontiers expand the capacity that defines the next ones — is not a utopia this book proposes. It is a configuration this book’s arithmetic prices, and the gross return is positive and exponential. What the investment costs, and how much of the return reaches the one who paid, depend on the case, and two cases are in hand. Between two towns of readers that send each other their surplus, famine falls twenty-fold for both: the return reaches the giver (code/two_towns_aid.py). And where steadier schedules were assigned by lot, the stores that gave them sold more (Chapter 13 §2D): there the investment cost its maker less than nothing. What any society does with that line item was never this book’s to say.

One thing more belongs on this side of the rule, because it is where the argument over any remedy will be fought. Which remedy helps depends on how the score is kept, and there are three ways to keep it; §5C runs all three inside the economists’ own model. Count what each household gets to consume, one household at a time, and cash wins easily: a steadier schedule barely registers. Count the capacity to plan, and the order reverses — time first, a steadier schedule second, cash nowhere. Ask whether the town survives, and it reverses the same way: the printed town starves in 11 seasons of a hundred with no program, in 11 with the cash, in 4 with the steadier schedule, and in fewer than one with the time. Which score to trust is a premise no model supplies. It is the same bridge §5 left to the reader — and two people can read the same three scores, choose differently, and each say exactly what the other is protecting.

§5CInside the economists’ own model

The machinery, for those who want it

[NUMERICAL — a standard model with one block added; every constant the model’s; signs committed in writing before the runs.] A mechanism that lives only in its author’s toy is a mechanism the field can decline to read. So the time gate of Chapter 7, the schedule tax, and the scarcity drain were given their simplest macroeconomic form — a household whose capacity to plan recovers only with free time above a threshold, and is drained by schedule entropy and by scarcity — and placed inside the heterogeneous-agent model that is the working instrument of modern macroeconomics: a one-asset HANK, in the family of Kaplan, Moll and Violante (2018) and the sequence-space form of Auclert, Bardóczy, Rognlie and Straub (2021), with sticky prices, sticky wages, a central bank, a government budget, and markets that clear. What is tested there is that reduced form, not Theorem 16 itself. The household’s bandwidth is a state beside its assets and skill; it degrades the household’s own optimization in the two faces the scarcity literature describes — noisier choices, a shorter horizon — and it is fed by free time above the gate and drained by schedule entropy and by scarcity itself. In the spirit of Gabaix’s sparse households and Sims’s costly attention, with this difference: the quality of the planner is a depletable stock that other agents’ decisions can draw down. Switch the two faces off and what remains is the standard household on a discretized savings grid with a small decision noise — it converges to the toolkit’s own as the grid is refined and the noise removed (wealth within 1.3%, consumption within 0.1%, at the finest grid run). Every number below is the model minus that control, each at its own general equilibrium, with the fixed-price version printed beside it. (Code and receipts: code/rig/hank_port/, docs/RESULTS_HANK_v0.1.md, docs/RESULTS_STRESS_2026-11-09.md; the signs were committed in writing before the runs, with one dated addendum — the forecast ruling below.)

The section in six lines, for a reader who will not follow the model through:

  1. The mechanism survives prices. With the drain on, households want a seventh fewer assets, and the interest rate that clears the market is a third higher.
  2. A cut in interest rates moves output further in the drained economy where wages are sticky, and less far where households set their own hours.
  3. The unpredictability a firm chooses for itself is more than the amount that is best for everyone, and a charge of half a percent of the wage bill per unit closes the gap.
  4. In 688 economies drawn at random the interest-rate results hold in every one. The counts of households living hand to mouth depend on the constants.
  5. Whether cash, time or a steadier schedule helps most depends on what is scored: consumption, the capacity to plan, or the town’s survival.
  6. All of it rests on one supposition, printed with its date: that a household does not foresee its own depletion.

The block, written out (code/rig/hank_port/bw_hank.py). A household’s state is its bandwidth bb, one of four levels from 0 to 3, its skill, and its assets. Write xx for the depleted share of bandwidth. Bandwidth enters the household’s problem in two places and nowhere else — the temperature of its logit choice of next period’s assets, and the discount factor it plans with:

x=1−b3,κ(b)=κ0+κ1x,β(b)=β(1−τx)x = 1 - \frac{b}{3}, \qquad \kappa(b) = \kappa_0 + \kappa_1 x, \qquad \beta(b) = \beta\,(1 - \tau x)

Each quarter bandwidth can rise one level and can fall one level, the two draws independent (a household drawing both stays where it is):

P(rise)=p↑ if T‾−N≥Tgate, otherwise 0P(fall)=1−(1−Sω)(1−d[cash on hand<m])\begin{aligned}P(\text{rise}) &= p_{\uparrow} \;\text{ if }\; \bar{T} - N \ge T_{\mathrm{gate}}, \;\text{ otherwise } 0\\P(\text{fall}) &= 1 - (1 - S\omega)\left(1 - d\,[\text{cash on hand} < m]\right)\end{aligned}

NN is hours worked, T‾\bar{T} the time endowment of the household’s skill group, SS the schedule entropy set on the firm’s side, ω\omega that group’s exposure to it, and the last factor the scarcity drain. The control economy sets κ1\kappa_1 and τ\tau to zero, which leaves bandwidth moving and changing nothing. The naive household solves its problem as if bb were permanent; the sophisticated one forecasts the law above. Welfare is scored at β\beta, never at β(b)\beta(b).

The printed constants, per quarter (code/rig/hank_port/hank_ge.py):

At these constants the low-skill group’s free time is 0.80, under the gate, and the middle group’s is 1.05, just over it.

What survives prices. The channel cuts household asset demand by a seventh at the standard model’s prices; with the stock of bonds fixed, the economy clears at a real rate a third higher — the mechanism is transmitted into the interest rate, not washed out by it. A monetary easing moves output 1.8 times as far on impact as in the control: a population whose bottom optimizer is taxed is an economy with a steeper spending response, which is the macroeconomist’s own quantity — in the host where wages are sticky and output is demand-determined. In a second host, where each household sets its own hours against a wage that clears, the same economy responds less than the standard one (0.7 times), because the taxed optimizer’s hours answer the wage more sluggishly; the amplification is claimed for the first host and not for the second, and the interest-rate result holds in both. (That is for small easings. At a hundred basis points the two economies of the second host respond alike, and at three hundred the taxed one responds a fifth more; most of the departure from linearity there is the lumpy choice of hours, which both share.) The fiscal counterpart is smaller. A tax cut paid for with debt moves consumption in both economies — neither household is the one that ignores such cuts, and most of that distance is the standard model’s own. The taxed economy spends a quarter to two fifths more of the cut within the year, more the longer repayment is deferred, and at fixed prices it spends less of it in the quarter it arrives, because decision noise blunts the constrained household’s one-for-one spending (code/rig/hank_port/ricardian.py). Schedule stability beats an equal-dollar transfer on hand-to-mouth status, under a condition stated below; which of the two leaves a household better off depends on how the score is kept, and is taken up further down; hand-to-mouth behavior persists after liquidity is repaired and recedes only when the drain is, under the same condition; a firm’s privately optimal schedule entropy sits above the planner’s, and the two coincide exactly when the channel is off, so the wedge is the externality and nothing else — a Pigou correction of half a percent of the wage bill per unit of entropy closes it at the printed constants. And the gate is live in the aggregate, in the first host: an easing large enough to push hours through a population’s time threshold produces an output response forty percent above its own linearization and a balance-sheet repair cut nearly in half, while the linear version of the same model, which is what the field computes, reports nothing at the gate at all.

What holds across the model’s constants, and what does not. The numbers above come from one set of constants, and a reader is entitled to ask how much of the section is that choice. So the constants were drawn at random — eight hundred economies across the whole box of noise, horizon, gate position, drains, debt, income risk, markup, utility curvature and both forecasts; 688 solved (code/rig/hank_port/sweep_signs.py) — and every signed claim was scored in each. Three held in all 688: asset demand falls at fixed prices; the real rate rises in general equilibrium; half the dose gives less than the full one. A fourth — more schedule entropy raises the rate further — held in all but five, each of the five a sophisticated household and each within a hair of zero. A fifth held in all but two of the 526 economies with the naive household: stability adds more welfare to the taxed economy than to the standard one by a wider margin than the equal-dollar transfer does — the part of the gain that belongs to the mechanism, not the whole of what a household gets. The hand-to-mouth claims are the ones that depend on the constants. With the naive household and the curvature of the printed economy they hold in nearly every draw — the taxed economy has more hand-to-mouth households in 97 of 100, the residual after liquidity repair is positive in 98, stability beats the transfer on that count in 88. With logarithmic utility, where the same decision noise is larger against flatter stakes, they hold in about half the draws — in seven of ten where the shortened horizon is large against the noise, in three of ten where it is small. The reason is the one the band already showed: the horizon face pulls households toward the limit and the noise face scatters them off it, and the count of households near the limit reports whichever is winning. The mechanism’s signature in the interest rate and in the stock of wealth does not depend on that contest; its signature on balance sheets does, and a field design that measured only hand-to-mouth status could find nothing, or the opposite sign, in an economy where the mechanism is fully present. One in seven of the drawn economies did not solve — the ones with little income risk and much public debt, not the ones with unusual bandwidth constants — and those are missing from every count here.

What prices reverse. At fixed prices a cash transfer beats a time transfer at lifting the time-poor out of hand-to-mouth status — the cash removes the scarcity drain and does the time transfer’s work; in general equilibrium that advantage shrinks by two thirds and the time transfer wins. The ranking of the two instruments is decided by the price adjustment, which is a warning printed for the field audit: a comparison that holds prices fixed can rank the arms wrongly. And in the second host, where hours are the household’s own, the cash wins on the balance sheet in general equilibrium as well — the time transfer’s gain there is bandwidth, not hand-to-mouth status — so the claim that time beats money at lifting households off the limit is made for one host and withdrawn for the other — and across the drawn economies of the first host it holds in two of five, so it is withdrawn as a general claim altogether. What survives is that the two instruments buy different things.

Where hours are the household’s own, three more things the one-asset host could not say. At the printed constants, nine in ten low-skill households work below their own time gate in the control economy, before any tax on bandwidth exists: the floor is sold for income, and the sale is not a symptom of the tax but its precondition. A freed hour is kept, not sold back — hours move by half a percent — and the share working below the gate falls by fifteen points. And a cap on long shifts lowers output and welfare in both economies and leaves the share below the gate where it was: the instruments this book prices are stability and time, not prohibition.

And a third host, for the objection that one asset is one too few: two accounts, a liquid one and an illiquid one that pays more and charges a fee to move — the structure the field uses for the wealthy hand-to-mouth (code/rig/hank_port/bw_two_asset.py; fixed returns unless said). There the head count of hand-to-mouth households barely moves, 45 percent against 47, while its composition turns over: the wealthy hand-to-mouth fall from 26 percent of households to 18 and the poor hand-to-mouth rise from 19 to 29. Illiquid wealth falls by a fifth and liquid by a seventh, and the liquid rate that clears its market rises a point and a half a year. The shortened horizon does this and the noise does not: the taxed household stops building the asset that takes patience. Repairing liquidity widens the low-skill gap, 16 points against 12. Time and stability lower low-skill hand-to-mouth status and raise illiquid holdings; an equal-cost cash transfer raises hand-to-mouth status in both economies and lowers illiquid holdings.

The constants of this host were then drawn at random, as the first host’s were: three hundred economies over the bandwidth constants, the income process, curvature, both returns, both fees and patience; 273 solved (code/rig/hank_port/sweep_two_asset.py). In every one of the 182 whose standard twin holds illiquid wealth worth a quarter’s income or more, illiquid wealth is lower under the tax — by a quarter at the median — and half the dose does less; in all but one the wealthy hand-to-mouth are fewer. Liquid wealth is lower, and the rate that clears it higher, in six of seven. The poor hand-to-mouth are more numerous in nine of ten and the head count is higher in five of eight: the composition is the signature, the count is not. The residual after liquidity repair is positive in five of six — nearly always at the printed curvature, in three of five under logarithmic utility. Stability raises low-skill illiquid holdings in 97 of 100, and equal-cost cash lowers them in all but one. A time transfer does its work only where it carries the household across the gate: where it does, illiquid holdings rise in nine of ten; where it stops short, in 2 of 71 — the time gate of Chapter 7, found again by a random draw. In the other 91 economies the standard twin holds almost no illiquid wealth. There is nothing there for the tax to remove, the noise scatters households upward off the floor, and the signs fail; they are mostly economies of logarithmic utility in which four households in five already live hand to mouth, and they are printed as the map’s edge.

Which remedy helps depends on how the score is kept, and there are three ways to keep it. The standard way counts what each household gets to consume over its life, one household at a time. On that score cash wins easily and a steadier schedule barely registers — at the printed constants it is worth to the household what a fifth of one percent of average income, paid in cash, is worth — because the only harm this score can see in a drained mind is a slightly worse savings plan, and slightly worse savings plans cost little (Cochrane 1989). The second way counts the capacity to plan, which in this host is bandwidth: the time transfer lifts the low-skill group’s from 0.30 to 0.65, stability lifts it to 0.42, and cash leaves it where it was. The third way asks whether the town survives. Put the same households in Chapter 11’s boats, on the supposition that a reader’s accuracy rises with bandwidth — a supposition with a measured direction: money worries cost a mind, on the spot, about what a lost night’s sleep costs it (Mani and colleagues 2013), and factory workers paid early by lot made fewer mistakes and turned out 7 percent more (Kaur and colleagues 2024). The direction has been measured in a laboratory, at a harvest and on a factory floor, and missed once, in a survey of American households around payday (Carvalho, Meier and Wang 2016). The town starves in 11 seasons of a hundred with no program, in fewer than one with the time transfer, in 4 with stability, and in 11 with the cash, because moving fish from one hold to another puts no boat on the fish (code/joined_three_rulers.py). And when a quarter of the fleet reads a little worse — right 60 times in a hundred where it was 70 — a ledger that adds up boats one at a time records 3.6 percent less fish, while the town’s famine rate more than doubles. Across the drawn economies the order holds: stability beats equal-cost cash on the standard score in none of the 528 economies of the first host and 4 of the 182 of the third, and on each of the other two scores in all but one.

The standard score is the only one of the three that favors cash, and the only one that counts each household as failing alone. Which score to trust is a premise no model supplies, and the sizes are the models’ own; the working — the two-asset figures, every version of the supposition, and what the earlier rankings “on welfare” in this section do and do not measure — is in Appendix H.

And one supposition, made explicit because every model of this kind carries it silently. The standard household knows its own mind perfectly and never degrades. A household that forecasts its own degradation — that plans around its future, more impatient selves — saves to protect itself from them, and in that model the repairs lose their effect or reverse it: a time transfer that lifts the group’s bandwidth by half leaves hand-to-mouth status where it was, and schedule stability raises it. A household that does not perceive the tunnel from inside, which is what the scarcity literature describes, saves less when degraded and more when repaired, and the repairs help. The two assumptions change the sign of the policies in the model; the second is the one used, and the first is printed beside it with the date on which the choice was made. A second premise is printed with the first: welfare is scored at the undegraded horizon — the degraded planner is a worse planner, not a person with a new preference. Any criterion that honors the shortened horizon as a preference scores the loss of bandwidth as a gain, because a more impatient household reports less concern for the hardship it is storing up; under such a criterion the planner’s schedule entropy rises above the firm’s and the correction becomes a subsidy to the drain. The Pigou result stands on the first criterion, and whoever prefers the second must own what it implies: that scarcity improves a life by that life’s own lights. A model’s suppositions about what its agents know of themselves, and about how their welfare is to be read, are not laundered into its conclusions here; they are listed, and the reader can see which conclusions depend on which.

A third supposition is the host’s own and is left as found. Its households’ skill is a number drawn by chance and redrawn by chance; nothing a household does, and nothing done for it, produces it. A reader who takes this model’s high earners for the talented is reading a lottery, and so is a reader who takes them for the lucky: the model cannot tell the two apart, because it has no account of where skill comes from. The towns of Chapter 11 have one — a reader’s accuracy fades with disuse and returns with practice — and no chapter of this book treats a capacity as issued at birth, or as equal at birth. Both are suppositions, and neither is needed.

Two cautions from the same host, found by stressing it. Hand-to-mouth status in every sentence above is a band — liquid savings within a fortnight’s income of the borrowing limit, as the field measures it — and not the limit itself: noise moves households off the exact corner into the band beside it, so counted at the corner the taxed economy shows less hand-to-mouth than the standard one and the stability result reverses; counted as the field counts, it holds. The same result asks one more thing of the mechanism: that the degradation touch the horizon or the attention and not the choice noise alone — four microfoundations of the degraded optimizer were run at equal footprint (noise, which is the rational-inattention solution; tunneling; present bias; sparse attention), and every one amplifies the monetary transmission in the first host, but under pure noise the stability arm and the transfer arm tie. And the economy’s own transmission is a function of the schedule regime — the monetary response is 1.4 times the standard model’s at half the printed entropy, 1.8 times at the printed one — so a response estimated under one regime does not carry to another, which is the economists’ oldest objection to reduced forms (Lucas, 1976), returned here against any audit that would estimate the mechanism’s effects from a single regime.

The constants are the model’s. Every bandwidth parameter is a model constant rescaled from an earlier toy; the gate’s position was placed by hand; the magnitudes — two to four points of hand-to-mouth status, under half a percent of consumption, a real rate higher by a median of eight tenths of a point a year across the drawn economies — are the model’s and not the field’s. What the section establishes: the mechanism is hosted by the standard model without modification to the standard model, and what it does there is computable, and it was computed.

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing

Every rule’s derivation, by chapter above; every constant’s model class in docs/THEOREMS_v1.md; every computation in code/, with the general-equilibrium host under code/rig/hank_port/.
