§1The rule of this chapter

Every question below is open for a stated reason: a proof nobody has found, a computation larger than any yet run, or a measurement nobody has taken. Each entry says which, and what closes it. Several entries that stood here in earlier drafts were closed by doing the work, and are kept as they were closed.

§2Proofs

The machinery, for those who want it

The exact frontier, and the plateau’s edge. The first curve for the trade between aim and unreadability was printed as within a hair of the truth. It was not: near perfect unreadability the plateau runs at least five times further than that curve knew (Chapter 6, the second kept corpse). The edge is now bounded below in closed form (0.247 in the reference world) and, numerically, by a vertex search (0.335) — the edge is a vertex of a polytope, which is why smooth optimizers missed it twice — and above only crudely (0.56); the exact edge, and the frontier’s shape from the edge to the sage point, are open. The vertex found at 0.335 recurred in fewer than one in a thousand of 127,000 restarts, which says the landscape has many local vertices and the true edge may be higher still. One case is now closed and one is fenced, by branch-and-bound on the separable concave objective (code/rig/plateau_edge_bnb.py). With three futures at a coin-noisy room the edge is exactly 1−1/log23≈0.3691 - 1/\log_2 3 \approx 0.369 — every future answered by an even split over two of the three actions — and the search tree is exhausted. With four futures the edge is fenced to the fourth decimal: the best vertex found, (5log25+9log23−6)/64≈0.31054(5\log_2 5 + 9\log_2 3 - 6)/64 \approx 0.31054, against a certified ceiling of 0.31074 after four million nodes. Vertices at more futures are floors, and the edge is not monotone in the number of futures: 0.369 at three, 0.311 at four, at least 0.357 at five — lower at four than on either side, with certainty. At five the certified ceiling after eleven million nodes is 0.469, so whether five sits above or below three is open. The floors found at six and seven, 0.335 and 0.359, continue the sawtooth, odd counts above even, without proving it. No formula that only falls or only rises with the number of futures can be the edge. For the reference world itself the same tool does not bite: after nine million nodes its certified ceiling at six futures is 0.641, looser than the crude 0.56 above. What closes it: a bound that tightens faster than the corners multiply. It is a problem in concave minimization over a polytope, stated completely, with certified floors printed for whoever takes it up.

The inversion on the wider plateau — posed here in one draft and answered in the next, kept as a worked example of this list shrinking. The inversion survives on the wider plateau (0.65 against the open expert’s 0.75) but the coin share a watcher needs rises from one-third to seven-tenths, because those strategies spend their chance where the world is wrong and the future is not for sale. The general law followed the same day — Theorem 9′, the sandwich — and the entry is kept as what it is: an open problem that lived for one draft.

The gate, generalized — closed. The threshold e+s>1e + s > 1 was proven for the symmetric worlds; for any channel the gate is a threshold per signal, e*=(qmax−qk)/(qmax+(n−1)qk)e^{\ast} = (q_{\max} - q_k)/(q_{\max} + (n-1)\,q_k), by the same four lines (Theorem 5c). Kept as a worked example of an entry that was open for one draft.

The wiring theorem, hardened — mostly closed. The dichotomy is now a one-parameter law: the floor depends only on how far the fresh bits reach across the choice space, exactly, across every habit-space size tested, and the one-time-pad point scales as the logarithm of the habit count (Theorem 11′). The gated inversion’s margin, which fails in one world of six on the wider plateau, turned out to be a coarse-habit effect: for fine habits the gated floor converges to a value below the ceiling at every hh (Theorem 11′(iv)). Open: the general theorem for arbitrary habit structures, beyond the span family.

§3Models

The machinery, for those who want it

The living town, continued. Chapter 11’s sixth lesson built the learning town and scored the standing prediction (refuted as stated; confirmed once crowding costs something). Fishers who consult yesterday’s sea are Theorem 21; fishers who may stay ashore are Theorem 23. What remains is the glass-sea reading — whether economies in which crowding costs nothing really do lose their self-correction — and that is a measurement: the same herd, observed where joining it is free and where it is not.

The clever weak watcher — closed. Run on the rig: pattern-miners with no model, and sequence models told nothing, reach the exact floor within days on every wiring and habit space tested (Theorem 20). There was no gap for cleverness to occupy; the entry is kept as what it was.

Acting and reading — modeled, not proven. Theorem 13 protects a town through its independent readings, whoever dispatches; a dispatcher who polls the fishers inherits it. Whether readings stay independent in a population that never acts on them — whether calibration requires one’s own mistakes — was the conjecture. As a model (code/rig/living_town_skill.py): let a fisher’s accuracy fade toward chance on days he follows and recover on days he acts on his own reading. The natural expectation, a point of no return, fails: a town of readers and a broadcast town reach the same long-run state, and the refutation is kept. What exists instead is a slope: with the strongest crowding the town keeps a third of its boats reading even when fading outruns recovery tenfold, but their skill is at chance, so the town looks plural and knows nothing the hub does not; with any slack in the crowding, fading at a fifth of a percent a day against recovery at half a percent carries the town from half-and-half to seven boats in ten behind the hub, and a glass sea, three-quarters herded to begin with, to nineteen in twenty. Two consequences. A head count of who follows cannot see the loss — it shows on the aim ruler and not on the independence ruler, which is the reason the book carries two. And because the state is an attractor and not a trap, it moves when its causes move: crowding restored or practice restored, the readers return. Whether human calibration fades this way, and how fast, is a measurement, not a theorem; the model says what would follow if it does.

The masters who lie, and the days that remember — computed in part. Persistent error, strategic misdirection and shared blindness are now in the town (S2, Chapter 11 §5): the dose rule survives as “follow the channel whose errors are independent of the rest, in proportion to its margin net of its lies,” and the all-readers headline is confined to readers whose errors are their own. Fishers who use yesterday’s sea are Theorem 21, and a master who misdirects once his following pays him to is computed (Chapter 11 §5). Readers who can tell are Theorem 22: they keep two tallies.

The surveillance regress — measured, not closed. Hypothesis; then the method that updates hypotheses; then the method’s inspiration — each level of watching must acquire a new private top level. The race between the fresh-input stream and the watcher’s acquisition now has one measured leg: a coin that is secretly a generator stays a coin only while its hidden state exceeds what the watcher can learn in a lifetime — between 12 and 32 bits for a million-parameter learner and the weakest generators (Result R6). The general statement, for any generator and any watcher, and what plays the generator’s role for a human mind, stay open. (Its speculative capstone — whether any watcher inside a universe can hold the whole of what feeds a mind — stays fenced where Chapter 12 left it.)

The household’s knowledge of its own mind. Chapter 14 §5C showed that whether a household forecasts its own degradation erases or reverses the bandwidth repairs in the standard macro model. The scarcity literature says the tunnel is not seen from inside; whether people are naive or sophisticated about their own bandwidth — and whether the answer differs across the gate — is a measurable question that no model can settle and that decides which of two economies the world is.

The bill’s counterfactual. Identifying a loss of aim is not attributing it. Attribution takes a design: the same person across time, a law that changes one place and not another, or assignment by lot. All three now exist for schedules (Chapter 13 §2D). What no dataset yet links is the schedule, the hours left over, and what the person went on to do with them — the column that would put a number on a time gate. It requires a panel that records all three; no public one does.

The leapfrog. The frontier is defined at current system capacity; agents who reach it expand the capacity, which relocates everyone’s frontier. A dynamic model of that recursion — growth as frontier expansion, theft as compounding foreclosure — is the next model to build. It needs one rule, for how a reached frontier moves the others; the two towns of Chapter 14 §5B are its first data point; and it is where this ledger meets the economists’ oldest question on their own ground.

The isolations still assumed. Each Part of this book removed an isolation the Part before it had assumed — the unwatched agent, the private error, the fixed accuracy, the private signal, the fixed price, the household that fails alone — and in most cases the conclusion changed with it (docs/ISOLATION_AUDIT_v1.0.md lists them). Two more were computed as this list was being written. A town with a neighbor: two towns of readers that send each other their surplus cut famine from 7 seasons in a hundred to a third of one, while two towns each behind its own master, or both behind one, gain nothing — aid is worth what the sameness between giver and receiver leaves it (code/two_towns_aid.py, exact). And who is on call: selling the burden to the same few boats is better for the town than drawing it by lot in most cases computed, because spreading it wears down every reader’s skill; the lot wins only where skill fades slowly and an on-call day is half lost; and the boats that sell end at chance, which the town’s famine count does not see. The expectation that such a trade would starve the town was refuted, and is kept (code/duty_trade_exact.py). Still assumed, with what removing each takes: a future that nobody’s action moves (the leapfrog, above); an education that arrives from nowhere and is independent of the world it is used in (a model of who teaches, and what it costs them); an agent who knows exactly how reliable its world and its own knowledge are (Theorem 22 is the first case in which it does not); a watcher who is not watched back (two-sided watching); a sea that is never fished down (a stock the fleet draws on); a skill drawn by lot (skill produced by time and teaching); uncertainty that travels down a hierarchy and never back up (quits and slowdowns in the cascade). Each is a model to build, not a measurement to wait for. One number would join the three scores of Chapter 14: what a unit of the capacity to plan is worth in consumption — this book’s title, asked as a number. That one is a measurement: the same people’s judgments, scored under a steady schedule and under a broken one. Seattle’s law measured their sleep and their hardship; nobody has yet scored their judgments.

§4Measurements

The machinery, for those who want it

The field audit. Three of its columns are filled (Chapter 13 §2D): strain follows who holds the schedule in a national survey, and within the same person across years, and the households on such schedules are paid less, not more; a scheduling law lowered hardship where it passed and not elsewhere; steadier schedules, assigned by lot, sold more. Not yet measured anywhere: a time floor, a gate distance, aim. What a survey of them can resolve was computed before any is run (code/rig/audit_identification.py): from one cross-section with free time measured to a tenth of its range, a sharp gate is told from a slope with near certainty at three thousand workers, and a ramp a quarter of the range wide still reads as a gate at ten thousand — the audit can establish that the tax arrives as a threshold, not how sharp the threshold is. Any comparison of time against money must hold prices or model them, because the ranking reversed between the two in Chapter 14 §5C. What the audit requires is not mathematics: a panel of a few thousand workers with schedules, free hours and outcomes linked. It is the largest project the book names, and the one on which its economic claims stand or fall.

The price of subtracting sameness. Decorrelation is worth more than growth past modest size — but diversifying teachers and breaking mirrors costs something, and that cost is a measurement no town can supply: what a second curriculum, a second feed, a second method costs to run. A ledger needs both columns.

The neighbors’ map. A full accounting of where this framework’s pieces were anticipated — the mathematics of influence, of limited attention, of unbreakable codes, of undiversifiable risk — is printed as Appendix D, and the news is good: nearly every part of the engine was built and tested elsewhere before this book borrowed it, which is the best thing that can be said of any part. The configuration is this book’s. The ancestors are named in the chapters where their shapes appear, with the difference stated each time, so that no reader mistakes similarity for identity in either direction.

The strongest standing attack, printed at full strength. Any quantum-scale slack, a critic will say, decoheres in the warm wet brain long before it could steer a neuron, let alone a schedule: the license may be real and the tenant impossible. The response has two parts. First, the in-principle version of the attack fails: classically chaotic systems amplify arbitrarily small differences to macroscopic scale (Borel’s electron at the edge of the universe altering a billiard break within seconds), and the brain is nothing if not nonlinear — so “too small to ever matter” is not a theorem anyone holds. Second, and printed with equal weight: amplification of noise is not harvesting of structure — chaos amplifies thermal jitter as happily as quantum slack — so sensitivity arguments establish possibility, never actuality. Whether any biological mechanism exploits the licensed asymmetry is a genuinely open empirical question, this list’s deepest entry, and the book’s claims are built to survive either answer: the ledger of Parts II-V measures apparent non-determinism relative to observers, and that quantity exists and is stolen regardless of which microphysics feeds it.

§5The oldest question

Untouched by any theorem in this book: whether the door the physics left open has anyone walking through it. The staircase and its ceiling license the possibility this book measures; they do not, and cannot, certify the tenant. That question stands where it has always stood — and for the first time in a century, it stands open, with no one entitled to close it by authority.

§6The invitation

Every result herein reproduces from the scripts in the repository; the corpses of the refuted conjectures are in there too, unembalmed. Check the arithmetic. Break what you can. What survives the attack is yours to use — that is the entire method, and perhaps the entire hope.

The invitation is not only to people who run scripts. The largest measurement this book names is in no repository: who holds the schedule, how much notice comes with it, what one mistake costs at the bottom of a hierarchy, which records keep plain days and hard days in one tally. Those are known first by the people living them — a cashier, a nurse, a line cook, a manager — and they enter the record when someone asks. So here is the instrument with the mathematics taken out: five questions that anyone can put to a rule, a bill, a workplace or a news report. None needs the mathematics. Each is what the mathematics said to look at.

  1. Who holds the eraser? Not whether the hours vary: who can change them, and on how much notice. (Chapters 7, 13.)
  2. What does one mistake cost here? One bad month from ruin, a person rightly waits to be nearly certain before acting on what they know. (Chapter 5.)
  3. One ruler, or two? Unpredictable is not free, and orderly is not fine: ask whose aim the hours serve. (Chapters 4, 7.)
  4. How many heads were there, really? Three forecasts that began from one source are one forecast. (Chapter 11.)
  5. Which tally, and which score? A record that mixes easy calls with hard ones flatters whoever made the easy ones; a remedy scored one household at a time has not been scored for the town. (Chapters 11, 14.)

Coda

The Whole Argument, Walked Once

Fifteen chapters is a long walk, and the path turned many times. So before the appendices, here is the entire argument again — every link in one chain, each tagged with exactly what holds it, walked from the particle to the monument without stopping.

Link one: the staircase, and its ceiling. Experiments violate Bell’s inequalities; something must give. If what gives is measurement independence — the assumption that the universe does not rig the questions to fit the answers — then the relaxation has an exact minimum price: F=R/(2(R+1))F = R/(2(R+1)), climbing a staircase with the number of particles, toward a ceiling it can never reach. F≤1/2F \le 1/2, at every size, forever. The universe’s statistics never require more than half of that independence to be given up. Total determinism-by-conspiracy is never forced. [PROVEN — the published record this book stands on.]

Link two: the door is lawful. Therefore a universe containing apparent non-determinism — agents whose actions are partly independent of their circumstances — is not a fantasy tolerated by physics but a standing possibility priced by it. The sentence “your freedom is an illusion, physics proved it” is revoked as authority; what remains of it is an opinion, holding a price sheet it rarely mentions. [PROVEN that the door is open; nothing yet about who walks through.]

Link three: congruence, claimed carefully. Which exit did the universe take? No one knows, and this book never pretends to. But notice the asymmetry in what each exit must explain. Your daily experience — that deliberation does something, that an hour of thought changes the evening, that people surprise you in ways that matter — proves nothing by itself. Yet the half-open exit accommodates that experience at zero cost, while the closed exits must explain all of it away, every day, in every life. A universe that took the door is congruent with the existence you actually have — and it is worth saying what that congruence consists of. This exit requires no influence traveling faster than light. It requires no endlessly multiplying unobservable worlds. It requires no cosmic conspiracy reaching into every laboratory, and no daily explaining-away of the lived experience that deliberation does something. Every exit from the experiments carries a cost; the other exits’ costs are real but unpriced. This is the only exit whose cost comes with a receipt — a posted, bounded price, never exceeding one half. And the receipt has since acquired a property no other exit’s cost possesses: it is collectible. The sequel to the staircase [arXiv:2608.18886] found the surviving local accounts’ bill split between two internal ledgers — measurement dependence and detection — with an exact exchange rate between them along the solved family, and posted a laboratory protocol whose outcome bounds that family either way, an order of magnitude below where the record now leaves it — and leaves the door’s price exactly where Chapter 2 proved it. Not the cheapest exit — the exits remain unranked, and the surface prices trade-offs within the surviving accounts, never across the exits. The only exit under audit. Congruent, priced, and auditable: not proven, and this book never says otherwise. FRAMING, not a theorem

Link four: the promotion. And here the whole project turns. Once AND is lawful rather than fanciful, it stops being a topic for philosophy seminars and becomes a quantity — a thing that could be present in degrees, and therefore measured, and therefore stolen. Everything before this link was license. Everything after it is measurement. This is also the answer owed to the second sentence of Chapter 1: it matters whether you have free will, and this ledger is the measure of how much. [The hinge — and the reason this book did not begin measuring until the license was proven.]

Link five: the two rulers. Measured how? Not by unpredictability alone — the harbor taught that. The ferry captain, flawless and fully written by her timetable; the lost tourist, unreadable and going nowhere; the sailor, tacking upwind, disagreeing with every gust and arriving anyway. Freedom is the double score: independence and aim. Every theorem in this book lives on the plane those two rulers draw. [EXACT definitions; PROVEN fences — the sage ceiling, the complementarity of what circumstances know.]

Link six: the anatomy. On that plane, agency turned out to have load-bearing structure, none of it guessed in advance and some of it found in the wreckage of refuted conjectures. The driver at the darkened intersection: education buys nothing until it beats the world — a gate, not a slope, sitting exactly at e+s>1e + s > 1, higher the more orderly the world. PROVEN Ines at the card table: perfect unreadability with real winnings exists — a plateau, wider than this book first printed — and past its edge, tells are the posted price of winning. [PROVEN; the edge itself OPEN.] The manager who steals nothing: the cheapest theft of freedom destroys aim and leaves unpredictability untouched, invisible to the single ruler of unpredictability; and a stolen hour lands on the order of a hundred times harder at the bottom of a time budget than the top. EXACT

Link seven: the watchers. Freedom carries a silent subscript — from whose seat — and making it speak produced the strangest exact result in the book: Theo with his three scores; Ines, inverted by the one watcher who sees her die; Elias, whose unreadability is one private conviction and who collapses completely the day it is learned. What looks like noise may be a hypothesis the watcher doesn’t hold — and privacy is not agency’s comfort but its wall. Against watchers with memory, Vera showed the wall’s engineering: it is not how many honest flips you make, it is whether your flips rule the big choices or only the details your habits already gave away. [EXACT; the two wirings the ends of one curve across every world built.]

Link eight: the towns. Then freedom went social, and the commons appeared. Priya, whose honest imperfection lowers her neighbors’ gates while consuming a bite of their ceilings; Aldo, never wrong and never hidden, beside whom every gate welds and every ceiling falls to zero. And the nine boats settled the question Aldo raised: nine okay readings beat one excellent reading six-fold, whoever gives the orders — the protection exponential in independent readings, annihilated by sameness (nine fishers, one tutor, exactly one head), dosed by hierarchy (at the printed margin, one follower of the master: medicine; five: poison), floored by whatever everyone shares, and insured, at the subsistence line only, by the wildcard nobody respected; and one more thing counted — a sage whose record was earned where the answer was easy and spent where it was hard. [EXACT, every famine probability; under masters who mislead, readers with bad weeks and shared blindness the structure held and the headline numbers did not — SIMULATION.]

Link nine: the ledger. A quantity that can be measured and taken can be booked. Theft — displacement off the frontier or of it — is an externality in the oldest sense: a real cost, imposed and uncounted, and what is uncounted is free, and what is free gets taken without limit. The manager came back with the strongest defense the position affords — I priced it in; they agreed — and left with four answers, the deepest being that the consent he cited was purchased with the very currency he took. He was never called evil. He was called unaudited, the one charge a signature cannot answer. And placed inside the economists’ standard model, with prices free to answer, the mechanism was carried into the interest rate, not washed out — with the premises it needs, what a household knows of its own mind and how its welfare is read, printed beside its conclusions. Asked which remedy helps, the same model gave opposite answers according to whether a household’s mistakes were counted as stopping at its own door. [EXACT instrument; testable parking prediction; NUMERICAL in a standard macro host, constants the model’s; the field audit begun — a survey, a law, an experiment.]

Link ten: the monuments. And when the machine — two axioms, no morality anywhere in it — was asked what made agents capable and towns durable, it handed back: education for all; rest for the overworked, the poorest first; privacy; pluralism; distrust of concentrated authority; shelter for the stubborn and strange. The list from the monuments, derived by arithmetic that never read them. Perhaps morality is the species’ compressed memory of theorems it could not yet write down. The resemblance is no longer unarguable either way. It has numbers now. [The observation, stated once, and its printed mismatch beside it.]

That is the chain entire: a ceiling in the statistics of particles; a door held lawfully open; a quantity promoted from philosophy to measurement; an anatomy, a wall, a commons, a ledger; and at the end, arithmetic shaking hands with the monuments. No link claims more than its tag. Several links were bought with the corpses of assumptions most readers will bring — corpses buried nowhere — they are in the appendix, with the scripts, where you can dig them up and check the cause of death yourself.

The universe declined, at every size priced, to demand the whole of you. What you do above that floor was never this book’s to say. What it cost, who paid, and who took — that, now, is arithmetic.

Appendices

The receipts, for anyone who trusts nothing

The repository: https://github.com/RandomInternetPreson/price-of-agency; this draft, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24599088. Every path printed in this book — code/, docs/, figures/, design/ — is a path inside it, and a claim is cited by the book’s title, its draft number and that address.

A. The theorem file — docs/THEOREMS_v1.md, tags intact.

B. The self-administered referee report — docs/REFEREE_REPORT_v1.md.

C. Reproduction — code/ directory; every figure from a script. One command, reproduce.py at the top of the repository, re-runs the scripts and checks each number against the sentence of this book that prints it; its last report is REPRODUCE_REPORT.md.

D. The neighbors’ map — docs/PRIOR_ART_MAP_v1.0.md (every citation verified against the record; thirty-four parts inherited, six arrangements the book’s, three small results without ancestors). In brief: the agent is Ortega–Braun’s bounded-rational one; the aim ruler is Sims’s and Tishby–Polani’s relevant information; the independence ruler is Shannon’s equivocation, measured in the field by Song and colleagues; the frontier is in the spirit of the information bottleneck. Theorem 1 is in the spirit of Conant–Ashby; Theorem 5 of Bayes decision theory and informational cascades; the time gate of Wald and the scarcity literature; the mistake budget of organizational slack. Theorem 6 is Cachin’s perfect steganographic security. Chapters 8–9 are Shannon (1949) and Kerckhoffs. Chapter 11 is Condorcet, the correlated-jury theorems, the insurance hypothesis, the ideal free distribution and producer–scrounger games. Part V is Pigou, Coase, Hacker’s risk shift, Mas–Pallais, Porter, Beer and Simon, with the bullwhip effect as sibling. Three results found no ancestor — cheap theft as an information statement, noise-subsidized overshoot, and the nonmonotone escape gate — each small, each reproduced in the repository. The moiré mechanism’s nearest picture, named in the paper itself, is the supermeasured account of Hance, Hossenfelder and Palmer (2022) — measurement dependence living in a non-trivial measure on the hidden variables rather than in a causal link — with Garza and Hance (2025) deriving such a measure for a different model; the mechanism is in that spirit, and whether it is supermeasured in their strict sense is left open there, as here. Chapter 14 §5C’s host is the heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model (Kaplan, Moll and Violante 2018; Auclert, Bardóczy, Rognlie and Straub 2021); the faces of its degraded optimizer are rational inattention (Sims 2003; Matějka and McKay 2015), tunneling (Mullainathan and Shafir 2013), present bias (Laibson 1997) and sparsity (Gabaix 2014); the objection it returns to reduced forms is Lucas’s (1976).

E. The physics record: arXiv:2608.00124, v3 (the staircase, proven at every size and certified through n=22n = 22; the ceiling F≤1/2F \le 1/2); arXiv:2608.18886, v7 (the exchange-rate surface, the hiding theorem, the protocol, the moiré mechanism and the structure of its floor-attaining census); Zenodo DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.21445609 (staircase) and 10.5281/zenodo.24053426 (CHSH scripts, offset banks, censuses — version 6.0 of the deposit whose concept record is 10.5281/zenodo.23537610). The book cites these versions; earlier versions are superseded on the points listed in docs/PAPER_SYNC_REPORT_v0.23.md.

F. Lexicon — docs/LEXICON_v1.0.md.

G. The stress record — docs/STRESS_CAMPAIGN_v1.0.md (each objection, where it was run, what it did to the claim); docs/RESULTS_STRESS_2026-11-09.md; docs/RESULTS_HANK_v0.1.md and docs/HANK_PREREG_v0.1.md (signs committed before the runs, with the dated addendum).

H. Three rulers, and the assumptions of isolation — docs/RESULTS_THREE_RULERS_2026-11-10.md (the full working behind Chapter 14 §5C’s three ways of keeping score); code/joined_three_rulers.py and code/results/joined_three_rulers.md, with the same three scores across the drawn economies (code/rig/hank_port/results_sweep_rulers/, results_two_asset_rulers/); code/two_towns_aid.py, code/duty_trade_exact.py, code/borrowed_record.py, code/stay_ashore.py, code/attack_T22_T23.py; docs/ISOLATION_AUDIT_v1.0.md (each assumption of isolation in the book’s models: where a later Part removes it, what changed, and those still assumed).

I. A ruler for one schedule — web/calculator.html. One file, run on the reader’s own device and sending nothing. It asks nine questions about a job. It answers how often that job’s schedule lets a person be where they planned to be, at a family dinner as much as at a class, and how far two weeks’ notice reaches beside a fixed schedule; and, in the model of Chapters 5 and 7, how many of ten thousand people on that schedule finish a course, every class of it, for how many it then changes what they do, and which change helps the most of them. Its counts are the most the schedule allows: the people in it can already pay for the course and chose it well. The model inside it is code/calculator_model.py, which checks itself against Theorems 5b and 16.
